entries.title: Gabriela Jaquez provides a refresher on why the Sky drafted her at No. 5
entries.summary: <p>With six UCLA players drafted into the WNBA this season, <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/chicago-sky" target="_blank" >Sky</a> rookie <b>Gabriela Jaquez</b> rarely goes long without facing an old teammate. Last week, it was <b>Lauren Betts</b> and <b>Angela Dugalic</b> of the Mystics.</p><p>On Tuesday, it was her good friend <b>Kiki Rice</b>. Drafted by the Tempo one spot behind Jaquez at No. 6, Rice has had an impressive rookie season, running the offense and averaging 13.4 points.</p><p>But Jaquez won the matchup Tuesday night, scoring 18 points in the Sky’s 97-85 win over the Tempo.</p><p>“You can tell who she is every single time she steps on the floor,” Rice said of Jaquez. “She’s gonna play hard, she’s gonna find ways to score.</p><p>“She’s the kind of player you want on your team.”</p><p>Jaquez fell out of the Sky rotation midway through the season and averaged just seven points, so Rice owns the better stat line for the year.</p><p>But now that Jaquez is back in a starting role, she’s showed more of why the Sky bet on her, averaging 14 points in the last three games.</p><p><b>First timers</b></p><p>The Sky’s late-season focus on their younger players has given two recent additions a chance to play.</p><p>Development player <b>Morgan Maly</b> scored the first basket of her WNBA career against the Dream, then followed it with eight points and four rebounds against the Tempo.</p><p>“I’m just trying to come in here and learn and try to fit the system and what they want to do,” she told the Sun-Times before the game.</p><p><b>Kate Martin</b>, another development player whom the Sky picked up after the Sparks released her, also got her first minutes. The Edwardsville, Illinois native hit her first three in a Sky uniform and had her mom and her old trainer in the stands to watch her do it.</p>
entries.author: Alissa Hirsh

entries.title: CPD searching for man who sexually assaulted woman on Blue Line train
entries.summary: <p>Chicago police are looking for a man wanted for allegedly sexually assaulting a woman on the Blue Line Monday evening.</p><p>The woman was on a train near the 4000 block of W Irving Park Road at 6:38 p.m. when the reported attacker sat behind her and assaulted her before fleeing the train, police said.</p><p>Police ask anyone with information contact Public Transportation Unit detectives at 312-745-4447.</p>
entries.author: Sun-Times Wire

entries.title: Potential nor’easter threatens Cubs’ final regular-season series in Boston with possible playoff implications
entries.summary: <p>The only thing the Cubs might be paying closer attention to than the scoreboard this week is the forecast.</p><p>Where’s <b>Tom Skilling</b> when you need him?</p><p>A nor’easter – a powerful storm with heavy rains and strong winds, for us Midwesterners not familiar with the specifics of East Coast weather – could make its way to Boston this weekend, threatening the Cubs’ final series of the regular season against the Red Sox at Fenway Park.</p><p>“It sounds like lovely weather ahead,” team president <b>Jed Hoyer</b> joked Tuesday.</p><p>Even before the beginning of their penultimate series of the campaign, against the Marlins at Wrigley Field, what might happen this weekend was a prominent topic of conversation.</p><p>Not only are the playoffs set to begin next Tuesday, giving little time to squeeze in any makeup games, but the games could be all-important in ironing out the bunched-up NL wild-card standings.</p><p>The Cubs started Tuesday tied with the Padres for the No. 1 wild-card spot, both teams only a game ahead of the Phillies. Should they stay tightly packed until the weekend, those contests will place the three teams, as well as determine who gets home-field advantage in the opening round.</p><p>Right now, there are still four different possibilities for where the Cubs could play a best-of-three series: Chicago, Philadelphia, San Diego and Atlanta.</p><p>So getting those games played – rather than bumping any of them to the Monday in between the end of the regular season and the start of the postseason – would obviously be preferred. Otherwise, the Cubs could end up playing Monday on the East Coast and, though it’s just one of many possibilities, flying to the West Coast for a Tuesday game against the Padres.</p><p>Hoyer didn’t offer any comments on suggestions that game times get moved or that the games themselves get moved to another city altogether.</p><p>But the Red Sox are also bound for the wild-card round and wouldn’t want to deal with those headaches, either.</p><p>“We’ve been in touch with the Red Sox and MLB,” Hoyer said. “Nothing’s decided yet, but certainly, we’re aware it’s a really bad forecast. Those things change a lot, so we’ll monitor the weather. But certainly, it’s something that’s on everyone’s radar.</p><p>“Exactly which days are in jeopardy and those things are still moving around, so we want to let that sort itself out a little bit. But it’s good that the two sides have been having discussions since yesterday.</p><p>“Playing Monday is obviously not a positive for anyone. But we’re trying to work through the different scenarios. Everyone’s aware of it. It’s [only] Tuesday.”</p><p><b>Shota in Game 1?</b></p><p>Will the Cubs tab lefty <b>Shota Imanaga</b> as their Game 1 playoff starter?</p><p>There’s a lot to figure out before then, but the southpaw bolstered his case Tuesday, holding the Marlins to a single run and striking out seven in five innings of work.</p><p>After struggling in September last season, Imanaga has been strong in the final month this year, with a 1.96 ERA in his last four starts.</p><p><b>Man of Steele</b></p><p>Lefty <b>Justin Steele</b> could find himself, finally, back on a big league mound before the end of the week.</p><p>“The plan is for him to be an option [to pitch] this weekend, possibly,” manager <b>Craig Counsell</b> said. “We’ll see what this weekend has in store for us and what this weekend gives us and make a decision.</p><p>“He pitched really well his last outing. And most importantly, that’s a good feeling for him, to have success and feel like, ‘I threw the ball well,’ as you work through this process of working back. That’s a great sign.”</p>
entries.author: Vinnie Duber

entries.title: Donda West Way: A South Shore street is renamed for a Chicago 'village mom'
entries.summary: <p>A group of Chicago-bred hip-hop legends gathered for a South Shore reunion, and for a moment, they transported to their teenage years — making music in the living room of their chosen mom, Donda West.</p><p>“This is not just a story about Donda West's son,” said Chicago Public Schools Board member and rapper Che “Rhymefest” Smith. “This is really a story about a woman who raised a community of boys.”</p><p>West was known for being the mother of hip-hop artist Ye, formerly known as Kanye West. To many Chicagoans, she was also an English professor, a former Chicago State University department chairperson, a businesswoman, a Fulbright scholar — and as Smith would call it, a “village mom.”</p><p>The two-story blue house on the city’s South Side was both the Wests’ home and where Ye’s music career was launched alongside his childhood friends. Now signs on 78th Street between South Shore Drive and Coles Avenue, at two nearby intersections, bear Donda West’s name.</p><p>“I love my biological mama, and I'm so proud to have a village mom like Dr. Donda West,” Smith said, with the crowd erupting in cheers.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Enhancement-item" data-crop=""> <figure class="Figure"><a class="AnchorLink" entries.title: Chase Meidroth 'brings fire' to surprising White Sox team
entries.summary: <p>KANSAS CITY, Mo. – Once the third piece of the four-player package the Boston Red Sox sent over for Garrett Crochet in December 2024, Chase Meidroth has blossomed into <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/cubs/2026/09/21/cubs-white-sox-chicago-pete-crow-armstrong-pca-alex-bregman-munetaka-murakami-will-venable-mlb" target="_blank" ><u>the best second baseman in Chicago</u></a>.</p><p>If wins above replacement (WAR) can be trusted, Meidroth is the most valuable everyday man at the position in the American League, even before he drove in five runs in the first three innings Tuesday night at Kauffman Stadium.</p><p>Meidroth isn’t one to sing his own praises, but plenty will do it for him.</p><p>“He leaves it all out there,” said Kyle Teel, the White Sox headliner of that same trade. “He’s always going to bring everything he’s got, every single time.”</p><p>“He's a guy who brings fire,” said double play partner Colson Montgomery. “He does a lot of things that a lot of us can't do, and he plays the crap out of second base.”</p><p>Montgomery is referencing how on an offense built on power but also running the fifth-highest strikeout in the sport, Meidroth is a peskier, contact-oriented hitter who provides a frustrating change of pace to opposing pitchers. That said, much of Meidroth’s breakout is summed up by the diminutive infielder unlocking the power to drive his 16th home run of the season–easily a professional single-season high–an estimated 410 feet on Tuesday night.</p><p>Meidroth is often cited as a beneficiary of the<a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/white-sox/2026/09/09/white-sox-hitting-director-ryan-fuller-talks-offensive-improvement-and-the-development-that-remains-colson-montgomery-munetaka-murakami-miguel-vargas-chase-meidroth" target="_blank" ><u> White Sox’ emphasis on bat speed training</u></a>, though his numbers don’t reflect a huge jump, and the occasional power strokes he allows himself are buried amid a host of shorter, slower cuts, dictated by the game situation. He’s not one to get into the weeds about his swing mechanics, but his coaches are happy to talk him up instead.</p><p>“There's a few things you could point to, but it's also knowing before two strikes, what's he using?” said hitting director Ryan Fuller. “‘When can he take his best swing over the middle of the plate, rather than the contact-oriented one he does with two strikes. It’s him understanding the game better, game-planning, the way you train, picking his spots when he’s in the box of being able to let it go a little bit.”</p><p>Nine of Meidroth’s home runs have come in 58 games since the All-Star break, and he entered Tuesday slugging .440 in the second half, despite playing much of it with a sore left wrist that has often required a brace or wrap. You can imagine how much he has to offer on that subject.</p><p>“It feels good,” Meidroth said of his wrist after a two-homer game in St. Louis earlier this month.</p><p>“He's been playing through some things a little bit, and I think that's kind of affected his offensive numbers,” Randal Grichuk told the Sun-Times. “Not necessarily here, but you play with some guys that they take the day, they want the day off. That's not him at all.”</p><p>With his all-business approach to interviews and the field, Meidroth cuts an amusing contrast to the <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/white-sox/2026/09/18/sox-pitcher-mike-vasil-throws-for-first-time-since-tommy-john-surgery" target="_blank" ><u>bubbly persona of his in-season roommate Mike Vasil</u></a>. The rehabbing right-hander acknowledges the outward difference in personalities, but thinks there’s a lot missed behind the scenes.</p><p>“It's his ability to actually listen and learn, and ability to also admit when he doesn't feel right or is struggling, or knows he needs extra help,” Vasil said. “It kind of reflects on other guys too. Because he's constantly having conversations–whether it's with [third base coach Justin Jirschele] about defense, whether it's [Derek Shomon] about hitting, day-in and day-out–making adjustments to get better.”</p><p>As recently as last year, the White Sox internally suspected Meidroth would settle into a utility role by the time they reached contention. If the Red Sox thought differently, they wouldn’t have traded Meidroth after a dominant 2024 season in Triple-A.</p><p>But like this White Sox team he powers, Meidroth has shown that projections can only tell you so much.</p><p>“He’s still evolving,” said general manager Chris Getz. “We are here to guide him.”</p>

entries.title: Facing division leaders, Royals eyeing 'spoiler role' in final week
entries.summary: <p>KANSAS CITY, Mo. — After winning seasons the past two years, the Royals enter a season-ending six-game homestand at 67-89 and as one of the bigger disappointments in the league.</p><p>Simultaneously, the road to the American League Central title runs through Kauffman Stadium.</p><p>Following three games against the second-place White Sox, the Royals will end their season this weekend by hosting the division-leading Guardians for another three-game set.</p><p>“We want to ruin somebody's season,” Royals catcher <b>Carter Jensen</b> told the Sun-Times. “We want to spoil it for somebody else. We’re obviously not going to be in the playoffs, but we want to be there. So if we can fill that spoiler role, I think it’s fun and we can show we’re not done fighting.”</p><p>Beset by pitching injuries that have seen both their opening day starter (<b>Cole Ragans</b>) and closer (<b>Carlos Estevez</b>) lost for the season, the Royals entered Tuesday losers of seven of their last eight. But with the emergence of young hitters like Jensen (.847 OPS since the All-Star break) and Jac Caglianone, Kansas City has an offense that’s allowed them to compile a 29-30 second-half record up to the final week.</p><p>With the Guardians entering Tuesday with a one-game lead and the Sox holding the season-series tiebreaker, the Royals can obviously affect the AL Central race, but also size up where they stand against the division’s best entering the offseason.</p><p>“Losing those pitchers, a few starting pitchers and bullpen pieces, it's been kind of a revolving door,” Jensen said. “We've done a great job this second half of not caring who all is here. We're just going to do the best with what we have.”</p><p>For their part, the Sox seem to understand that ending their season against two last-place teams does not equate to a cakewalk.</p><p>“We are so close to making a huge difference, not just for us but for the history of the organization,” said <b>Miguel Vargas</b>. “Accomplishing what we want is going to be hard. It’s not going to be easy.”</p><h3><b>Vargas is AL Player of the Week </b></h3><p>Vargas was named American League Player of the Week on Monday, after hitting .348/.500/.783 with three home runs from Sept. 14-20. It’s Vargas’ second time winning the award, with the first coming in May last year.</p><p>The timing makes the second time around sweeter.</p><p>“We treat this as a playoff game,” Vargas said. “Whatever we did in the past five months wouldn’t mean anything if we don’t make it.”</p><p>The Sox roster largely hasn’t been through a playoff chase before, but Vargas looks like he has the ability to raise his game.</p><p>“We’ve seen him increase his attention to detail,” said manager Will Venable. “He’s absolutely locked in right now. And I think it’s a response to where we’re at.”</p><h3><b>Peters at the ready</b></h3><h3></h3><p>Four days after a scary collision with a Rate Field outfield fence post, All-Star outfielder <b>Tristan Peters</b> is at “full availability,” though he was out of Tuesday’s starting lineup against a left-handed opposing starter.</p><p>“To give his body up to try and make a play like that speaks a lot to the kind of player he is, and being able to recover from that so quickly has been awesome," Venable said.</p><p>In Peters’ stead, <b>Brenton Doyle</b> homered in his first at-bat against southpaw Daniel Lynch IV on Tuesday.</p>

entries.title: Indiana man charged after leading high-speed chase from Hammond to South Shore
entries.summary: <p>An East Chicago, Indiana man is facing charges after he led Indiana State Police on a high-speed chase from Hammond to South Shore Tuesday, according to police.</p><p>Austin Earl Williams, 37, was arrested on multiple charges, including burglary, robbery, strangulation, resisting law enforcement with a vehicle and two counts of domestic battery stemming from two different cases, according to state police. That’s in addition to misdemeanors for interference with reporting of a crime and domestic battery.</p><p>Additional charges are pending related to the chase, Indiana State Police said.</p><p>Williams had been wanted on multiple felony charges when Indiana State Police attempted to pull him over after his license plate was pinged by a <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/crime/flock-license-plate-reader-explainer" target="_blank" ><u>Flock license plate reader camera</u></a>, troopers said. He then reportedly fled before crashing at the intersection of 77th Street and East End Avenue.</p><p>Williams is set to appear for an extradition hearing in Cook County before being returned to Indiana, authorities said.</p>

entries.title: Griffin MSI's new design proposal is an affront to Chicago history
entries.summary: <p>Kudos to Sun-Times architecture writer <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/architecture-design/2026/09/21/griffin-museum-science-industry-design-ramsa-drawing-board" >Lee Bey’s perceptive critique of the Griffin Museum of Science and Industry’s damaging proposal</a> to alter the building's north facade. But if I could offer my own respectful critique of the critique, it didn’t go far enough.</p><p>The museum's current proposals to significantly alter both the building's north and south elevations display gross disrespect for a masterpiece of classical composition that generations of architectural commentators have deemed to be nearly perfect in composition, proportions and detail.</p><p>Created as the Palace of Fine Arts for Chicago's legendary World's Columbian Exposition of 1893, it is the sole intact major building surviving from this epoch in the city's history. This fact alone is reason enough to protectively respect its integrity. But the original architect, Charles B. Atwood, gave it even more. At the time of completion and for decades afterwards, it came to be regarded as perfection in its adaptation of Classical architecture — a challenging genre in which all parts must precisely relate to the whole.</p><p>Even when the building's temporary skin of hard plaster was to be removed and replaced with permanent limestone for its 1930s conversion into the Museum of Science and Industry, the renovation drawings firmly stated that all details were to be reproduced exactly to preserve its precisely composed architectural integrity.</p><p>The current museum proposal to remove or cut gap-toothed holes into the boldly scaled classical grand staircases and the glassing-in of both monumental entry porticos hardly reflects the respect given to this architectural masterpiece over the past 133 years, and the motives behind making it a protected city landmark.</p><p>Perhaps the only hope is for the guardian angels of great architecture to somehow make these damaging proposals disappear.</p><p><i>Tim Samuelson, Cultural Historian Emeritus — City of Chicago</i></p><div class="RichTextSidebarModule Enhancement" data-module data-align-center><a class="AnchorLink" id="module-6f0001" name="module-6f0001"></a> <div class="RichTextModule-items RichTextBody"><h3>Give us your take</h3><br>Send letters to the editor to <a class="Link" href="mailto:letters@suntimes.com" target="_blank" >letters@suntimes.com</a>. To be considered for publication, letters must include your full name, your neighborhood or hometown and a phone number for verification purposes. Letters should be a maximum of approximately 375 words.</div> </div><p></p><h3>Let Chicagoans sit again</h3><p>Bravo to Sam Kovnar and Eddie Lehwald of the Northwest Neighborhood Alliance for facilitating some return to sanity and hospitality in reinstalling seating at city bus stops ("<a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/transportation/2026/09/14/cta-bus-stop-bench-ukrainian-village" >This group is building benches at bus stops that don’t have one. Will the city let them stay?</a>").</p><p>Can we go further and return much-needed benches to parks, walkways and along city streets?</p><p>Is Chicago such a city on the go that pedestrians are not allowed to stop anywhere?</p><p>People-watching from her perch on a city bench was one of my grandmother’s favorite pastimes. Benches also provide much-needed rest when running errands on foot or going on long walks.</p><p>Contrary to the argument that they increase loitering, benches can actually deter crime by creating natural eyes and ears on the streets.</p><p>As for attracting those without a bed, do we close libraries because the unhoused may choose to spend time there? Where is our humanity in causing those who need a rest to sit on the sidewalk? Let Chicagoans sit again!</p><p><i>Ruth Solomon Tupper, West Rogers Park</i></p><h3>Why your vote matters</h3><p>We are Americans, and we vote! Lest you think your vote doesn’t matter, here are four reasons why it does:</p><p>It allows you to express your opinions and values and choose elected leaders who will make decisions on your behalf and whom you can hold accountable.</p><p>It supports strong schools. Voting helps choose leaders who decide school funding, classroom resources, after-school programs and the quality of education students receive.</p><p>It improves neighborhoods. Your vote shapes local housing, public transit, healthcare and community safety.</p><p>It lets you choose the judges who make decisions that can protect your rights, affect your families, and shape whether systems make people’s lives better or worse.</p><p>So, make a plan to vote, either by mail, at an early-voting site or in person on Election Day.</p><p>Voting is the foundation on which our very Democracy was built. To vote is a privilege and a right. Do not squander it!</p><p><i>Diane Edmundson, League of Women Voters of Cook County</i></p><h3>Make restaurant careers more accessible</h3><p>As Chicago works to <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/food-drink/2026/07/15/james-beard-awards-chicago-host-city-culinary-oscars-restaurants" >bring the James Beard Awards back</a>, we should consider how the city can lead the industry in expanding access to restaurant careers.</p><p>The industry must recognize that people with disabilities are a valuable part of the industry's workforce and a solution to the restaurants’ turnover crisis. More pathways must be created to connect them with employers.</p><p>Some Chicago-area businesses are already taking steps in that direction. For example, our industry partners are offering internships to participants completing Aspire's Food Services Employment Training Program, which prepares people with disabilities for front- and back-of-house restaurant roles.</p><p>Expanding access to restaurant careers can help employers build more stable teams, create meaningful employment opportunities and demonstrate to the rest of the country what the future of a strong culinary community can look like.</p><p><i>Serena Alaily, La Grange</i></p><h3>The AI education paradox</h3><p>If AI-powered cheating accelerates America’s educational decline, gullible administrators will share the blame. The University of Chicago, my alma mater, recently gave students and faculty free access to Anthropic’s Claude software. It is thus working not to educate students but to help them bypass education.</p><p>AI poses an unprecedented threat to education. Its purpose, evident in the term “artificial intelligence” itself, is to think so users don’t have to. But thinking is the point of education. Education is the product of the mental struggle for which AI offers itself as a substitute.</p><p>Schools build the knowledge, skills and habits of mind that help people solve complex problems and participate intelligently in society. These are built over time, through practice and feedback that gradually change students’ brains. Learning occurs through, and is inseparable from, the investment of time and effort.</p><p>AI encourages students to skip learning: upload your assignment, and the computer will do it for you. Never have students faced a more tempting but self-defeating escape from the woes of homework and grades, or a more addictive and mind-eroding drug. Schools should shelter them from it, not promote it.</p><p>The University of Chicago has always been a home for students who love to learn. Students talk about books and wear shirts extolling the Life of the Mind. It is a former Big Ten school that once bulldozed its football field and replaced it with a library. It now throws the bulldozer into reverse.</p><p><i>Ryan McCarl, attorney</i></p>

entries.title: Dear Abby: Unfaithful husband invites other woman to move in
entries.summary: <p><b>DEAR ABBY:</b> My husband, "Dirk," cheated on me more than 20 years ago. He has kept in touch with the woman since then. Sixteen months ago, she told him she was "in a bad place." He offered to let this (married) woman move in with us and didn't tell me until two weeks before she got here.</p><p>Abby, this woman lives like a pig. Her room is filthy, and she has broken several things in my house without paying for anything. Before she moved here, Dirk wanted to get her teeth fixed. I ended up paying for it with my credit card. She promised she was going to pay me back, but she has given me exactly $510 of the $5,000 that she owes me. She has a job, so there's no reason why she is not giving me the money.</p><p>I'm not worried about Dirk cheating with her again, as she has not maintained her looks or figure over the years. Still, how much more of this should I take? I asked her to leave once, but he got her to come back. He will not go to marriage counseling as he doesn't think we need it. When I ask him why he keeps her around, he tells me he enjoys her company. Do you think I should contact a lawyer and start divorce proceedings or let this go? — <i>LOSING MY MIND IN TEXAS</i></p><p><b>DEAR LOSING MY MIND:</b> My dear, you should have left long ago. Call a lawyer immediately. However, since this woman is not a physical threat, resist the urge to move out until you have your attorney's approval. Abandoning your home may harm your case in the divorce proceedings.</p><p><b>DEAR ABBY:</b> I became close with an attractive, younger co-worker last year. Realizing I was starting to get a crush, I told her I needed to stay away because of my feelings and, being married, couldn't risk losing my family. She went through a hard time during our breakup, but we started getting close again. The breakup led her to do something she regrets so much it has affected her work. It has alienated pretty much everyone she knows except for me. I have encouraged her to seek professional help because her emotional state is very draining. I also feel I have reached a point where I no longer want to be around it, but I don't know how to tell her without feeling guilty for turning my back on her when she's begging for help. She's in such a depression; she's killing herself slowly. What should I do? — <i>REMOVING MYSELF IN THE EAST</i></p><p><b>DEAR REMOVING:</b> What you should do is reiterate to her firmly, but as kindly as you can, that she needs to get professional help for her depression. If she balks, explain that, because of her emotional state, she has alienated friends and co-workers and that you are not equipped to give her the support she needs. Then learn from this experience and back away.</p><p><i>Dear Abby is written by Abigail Van Buren. For nearly four decades, Jeanne Phillips penned this column, which was founded in 1956 by her mother, Pauline Phillips. Contact Dear Abby at www.DearAbby.com or P.O. Box 270135, Kansas City, MO 64127.</i></p>

entries.title: Sweet Stash moves its Wonka-esque gummy production to Chicago
entries.summary: <p>More than a century after Wrigley, Brach’s and Mars helped turn Chicago into a candy epicenter, a trio of artists with an unabashed candy obsession brought their gummy candy startup to the shuttered former Jelly Belly plant in suburban North Chicago, ushering in a new era for this storied city of sweets production.</p><p>The actor Martin Starr and musicians and identical twins Ezra and Adeev Potash cofounded Sweet Stash last fall with an additive-free gummy with the complex flavor and texture dimension of candies they discovered over years of globe-trekking.</p><p>“We are obsessed with candy beyond what’s normal and maybe even healthy,” Ezra said. “We’ve been candy people long before we became candy vendors.”</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div This self-starting trio can also keep making candy limited mostly by their imaginations in a city known for confectionery innovation — a rarity for an industry dominated by profit-seeking conglomerates.</p><p>“We’re a small band of creative people going up against billion-dollar companies that make candy by the tank,” Adeev said.</p><p>On a hot and sticky recent Thursday, the bespectacled twins and I scooched into a taped-up booth beneath a wood-paneled wall full of bric-a-brac at the 105-year-old Margie’s Candies in Logan Square. The historic shop carries the original Jams, along with the crunchy sugar-coated Rock Jams and tart<b> </b>Sour Jams Sweet Stash that the trio launched this summer.</p><p>“If there’s a place we had to be in Chicago, it was here,” Adeev said. “This is an institution for a century. class="Figure-content"><figcaption class="Figure-caption"><p>“If there’s a place we had to be in Chicago, it was here,” Adeev Potash said. “...It’s a place that loves new things, but that also respects the history.”</p></figcaption><span class="line"></span><div class="Figure-credit"><p>Pat Nabong/Sun-Times</p></div></div> </figure> </div> </div><p>Adeev (trumpet) and Ezra (trombone) are musicians first, discovered and mentored by the trumpeter and composer Wynton Marsalis. They’ve released three albums and written scores for the likes of “RuPaul’s Drag Race.” They have also hosted television series for Travel Channel, Bravo and Food Network. As touring musicians, the twins (who divide their time between Los Angeles and Omaha) developed a habit of popping into bodegas after shows in search of candy they’d never tried.</p><p>“After years of doing that, we kind of became pseudo-experts on what was available to the public all over the world,” Ezra said. Apparently, candy invention is even in their DNA. In the 1800s their great grandparents owned Wolfberg’s General Store in Wakarusa, Indiana, where they said their great-grandfather, rather presciently, invented the giant jelly bean. </p><p>They met Starr in 2022 at a charity event, hosted by celebrities including Jason Sudeikis and Paul Rudd, where the trio became fast friends.</p><p>“It was late at night and I think somebody was eating Haribo Goldbears,” Adeev recalled, then Ezra interjected. “We probably said something nerdy, like, ‘I think they’re just the perfect texture, but the flavors are a bit flat.’ And then Martin was probably like, ‘What the hell did I just see?’”</p><p>“They didn’t even <i>like</i> candy until they met me,” Starr quipped, reached somewhere in New York on Ezra’s phone.</p><p>Known best for his role as the cynical, deadpan Bertram Gilfoyle on HBO’s “Silicon Valley,” Starr has worked as an actor and producer across television and film, including series like the Paramount drama “Tulsa King” (where Sweet Stash makes a handful of cameos), Starz’s “Party Down” and films including “Knocked Up” and “Adventureland.”</p><p>Starr’s candy obsession runs deep, too. He recalled as a kid eating gummy bears “to the point where my parents stopped giving me an allowance, because all I spent the money on was candy.”</p><p>A few months after they met, Starr invited the “the boys” to his home in L.A. (Starr also lives part-time in Austin, Texas.) Ezra and Adeev remained skeptical of Starr’s candy mania until they glimpsed his cupboards dedicated to candy from around the world, grouped by country and ingredient list, as in, vegan, containing gelatin and gluten-free. </p><p>“We’re like, we've actually met our match,” Adeev said. </p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Enhancement-item" data-crop=""> <figure class="Figure-content"><figcaption class="Figure-caption"><p>“We are obsessed with candy beyond what’s normal and maybe even healthy,” Ezra Potash said. “We’ve been candy people long before we became candy vendors.”</p></figcaption><span class="line"></span><div class="Figure-credit"><p>Pat Nabong/Sun-Times</p></div></div> </figure> </div> </div><p>What’s the ideal amount of chew in a gummy? Can one replicate the physical sensation of peach fuzz in a candy? What should the color green taste like? Such Wonka-esque questions increasingly occupied the minds of the three as their friendship deepened. They wondered why all the confections they love most, featuring layered flavors and invigorating textures, had to be imported from Japan or Australia. They lamented that American candy conglomerates were directing innovation budgets toward injecting sweets with fiber or protein rather than cleaning up their ingredient lists.</p><p>“If you want fiber, eat something natural that has fiber it; don’t put in my f------ candy,” Starr said.</p><p>They decided to join forces and start a candy company of their own, debuting with an American-style gummy made with high-quality ingredients, a texture that “bites back” and the flavor dimensionality of Japanese and Swedish candies they love. Using their own funds, they recruited candy scientist Tessa Porter, former chief innovation officer of Ferrara, to help develop the additive-free gummies. The designer Ellen Van Dusen, of cult housewares line Dusen Dusen, created the brightly colored packaging. In a nod to the public arts programs that were foundational to the trio’s careers, they donate a percentage of Sweet Stash’s profits to arts education <a class="Link" href="https://sweetstash.com/#conscience" target="_blank" ><u>initiatives</u></a>.</p><p>Jams come in six flavors — er, technically 18 if you ask Ezra — which took six months to develop. The three spent hours at a time hashing out each color and accompanying flavor journey. Take Prickly Pear, which starts out tart and pineappley then melony with a tropical, almost floral finish as your teeth slowly work through that springy confection (which by the way isn’t nearly as chewy as these nerds like a gummy). Or Grape, which can, in fact, be green. </p><p>“Sorry, but grape doesn't need to be purple and taste like cough syrup,” Adeev said, munching on a crisp Green Grape Rock Jam enrobed in fat sugar crystals. “It could actually taste like the best, juiciest grape you ever had in your life.”  </p><p>They expected to sell the candy online only until Rudd, who owns a sweets shop in New York’s Hudson Valley, asked to be their first retail customer. Before long, other indie retailers came calling with orders, then reorders. More than 300 specialty retailers nationwide now carry Sweet Stash, including 10 to 15 in Chicago, such as RAYGUN Clothing, Pop/Culture Chicago and the Chicago Athletic Association.</p><p>When it became clear Sweet Stash was rapidly outgrowing the Omaha facility, the founders pledged to keep production in the Midwest, which significantly shrunk the pool of plants that could produce a formulation of their standards at scale, they said.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Enhancement-item" data-crop=""> <figure class="Figure"><a class="AnchorLink" class="Figure-content"><figcaption class="Figure-caption"><p>Sweet Stash is an American-style gummy made with high-quality ingredients, a texture that “bites back” and the flavor dimensionality of Japanese and Swedish candies the co-founders love. </p></figcaption><span class="line"></span><div class="Figure-credit"><p>Pat Nabong/Sun-Times</p></div></div> </figure> </div> </div><p>“Production is already allotted to a lot of the big companies; we were lucky to find a place we could grow with in Chicago,” Starr said.</p><p>The North Chicago plant churns out 160,000 bags per month, four times the 40,000 bags produced over a months-long run at the Albion plant. With more sophisticated equipment, the team can also maintain precision and consistency over product texture and flavor as it scales and fulfills larger orders.</p><p>“It’s still crazy that we have a candy company,” Adeev said. “To see it made in a facility that’s been making one of the most famous candies for 100 years, it’s amazing.”</p><p> The move represents a bright spot for a city that has lately seen high-profile confectionery plant closures like Blommers’ and Mars Wrigley’s in addition to Ferrara, which shuttered the Jelly Belly plant in 2024. More sweet news came for Chicago in April, when the National Confectionery Sales Association announced that the city would house the permanent location of the 60,000-square-foot <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/museums-zoos/2026/04/09/candy-hall-fame-experience-museum-mag-mile" target="_blank" ><u>Candy Hall of Fame Experience</u></a>, at 830 N. Michigan Ave. It is slated to open in 2027. </p><p>As far as Sweet Stash is concerned, Chicago remains “Candyland USA,” Ezra said. “Every major candy brand is manufactured here, all the innovation is happening here.”</p><p> The latter now includes a trio of candy-obsessed artists, whose enthusiasm seemingly has them leapfrogging confectionery science in the name of whimsy, as they hinted about a potential gummy innovation “so out there that we have to literally wait for the science to catch up,” Ezra said. </p><p>Then again, maybe this industry of “billion-dollar Goliaths” needs a little more Willy Wonka energy.</p><p>“We’ve been told what we want to create is not possible all the time — as candy even more so,” Adeev said. “For us, making Sweet Stash is like being an actual kid in a candy store. How <i>do</i> you make an everlasting gobstopper? What’s the thing you can’t do?”</p><div class="RichTextSidebarModule Enhancement" data-module data-align-center><a class="AnchorLink" id="module-550000" name="module-550000"></a> <div class="RichTextModule-items RichTextBody"><h3>Flavor journey</h3><br>To bite into one of the six Sweet Stash gummy flavors (<b>categorized by tart and rich)</b> is to embark on a texture and flavor journey. <br><br>“We’re almost making a caricature of a flavor,” Ezra Potash said. “When you take a bite, it needs to be distilled into the spirit of that flavor while adding others into it that bring out the original.” <br><br>The gummy’s al dente chew prolongs said flavor journey, supercharged by the tart-sweet dust coating Sour Jams and fat sugar crystals on the sweet Rock Jams.<br><br><b>Prickly Pear (tart)</b><br>Sharp and pineappley to start, the journey turns melony before ending with a tropical, almost floral, finish that croons with pear.<br><br><b>Blue Jazzberry (rich)</b><br>The richest of the six and a crowd favorite, this spirulina-dyed blue gummy begins subtly before crescendoing with jammy, complex notes of fresh and cooked raspberry and blackberry.<br><br><b>Strawbarb (rich)</b><br>A gentle sweet-sour hum swells into that telltale springtime combo of juicy, brightly floral berry and puckering rhubarb with a crisp finish.<br><br><b>White Peach (rich)</b><br>A soft static mimics the lip-tickling fuzz on a peach before the sweet, gently tangy ripe stone fruit notes coat the palate in this clear gummy.<br><br><b>Orange (tart)</b><br>The clean, linear burst of citrus peel mingles with marmalade-esque stickiness in this multidimensional take on orange. “This almost didn’t end up in the bag because orange isn’t a flavor profile I gravitate towards — the boys felt similar,” Martin Starr said. “That went through the most rounds of testing. We ended up very happy.”<br><br><b>Green Grape (tart)</b><br>Like the snappy burst of crunching into a green grape, this green gummy ricochets gently floral stone fruit and citrus across your tongue, then coasts out with a hum. </div> </div><p></p>

entries.title: As school board election nears, CPS parents incensed by political group at school event
entries.summary: <p>Parents and other members of a Local School Council are asking Chicago Public Schools to sanction an organization that they say violated the district’s rules by electioneering at a back-to-school festival on school grounds.</p><p>Dad Adam Johnson, who has one child at Peirce Elementary School in the Edgewater neighborhood, said parents who walked up to an arts and crafts table hosted by the Common Ground Collective might have assumed it was a “kind of generic liberal, if not hippie-ish organization.”</p><p>But if they picked up a flier about the upcoming school board election and scanned a QR code, they’d see the organization was making endorsements, he said.</p><p>“The return-to-school celebration is, I think, supposed to be about the kids and about meeting the teachers, not about promoting a particular political agenda,” he told the school board earlier this month.</p><p>CPS strictly prohibits political campaigning on school grounds. CPS’ ethics office is investigating what happened at Peirce.</p><p>A spokeswoman for the Common Ground Collective said the group staffed a table and paid for the DJ at the Aug. 20 fair through its nonprofit, which is separate from the group’s two political arms. The spokeswoman also said the endorsements weren’t posted until after the Peirce Elementary event, pointing to social media posts timestamped on Aug. 24 as evidence.</p><p>The Common Ground Collective says it supported “multiple” back-to-school events, but CPS says it only received a complaint from Peirce’s LSC.</p><p>The controversy illustrates how schools have had to navigate some ethically thorny situations in the runup to the Nov. 3 election, when voters will elect all 21 members of the school board for the first time.</p><p>Some see this race as a test of whether anyone can wrest control from the powerful Chicago Teachers Union and Mayor Brandon Johnson, a strong CTU ally who appointed the majority of school board members.</p><p>As of Tuesday, $3.3 million has poured into the coffers of school board candidates. On top of that, political groups are spending on digital ads about candidates. Much of that has come from political action committees with ties to other entities and individual donors. That’s made it difficult for principals, parents and others to decipher who is truly behind an effort and whether it’s political in nature.</p><p>Others have raised concerns about electioneering, too.</p><p>Austin Berg, the marketing director for the Illinois Policy Institute, a nonprofit think tank that supports limited government and personal liberties, sent a complaint to the CPS ethics advisor about school board member Michilla Blaise, who is running to keep her West Side seat. Berg alleged that Blaise made a social media post in violation of the rule that prohibits board members from conducting political activity while doing their official work.</p><p>Blaise says the video showed students dancing and welcoming her to a school. She promptly took it down out of concerns for student privacy, but she says she posted it because she thought “it was so cute,” not as part of her campaign.</p><p>In response to the heightened concerns about electioneering, CPS said it “recently issued guidance” to principals and Local School Councils to <a class="Link" href="https://www.cps.edu/about/ethics/ethics-political-activities/" target="_blank" ><u>make sure they understand the rules</u></a>.</p><h3><b>Groups with nonprofit and political arms can confuse schools and voters</b></h3><p>Founded just a year ago, the Common Ground Collective is an anti-CTU group that is heavily funded by billionaire Michael Sacks, who was a top donor and adviser to former Mayor Rahm Emanuel. The group says it aims to engage voters around “effective progressive policies” and wants to ensure “taxpayer dollars are used wisely and effectively.”</p><p>So far, Common Ground Collective’s political groups, which include a political action committee and a super PAC that has fewer limits on contributions and spending, have donated about $31,000 directly to school board candidates. They’ve spent another $944,000 on digital ads supporting or opposing certain candidates.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Enhancement-item" data-crop=""> <figure class="Figure"><a class="AnchorLink" id="image-da0000" name="image-da0000"></a> <picture data-crop="medium"> <source type="image/webp" width="490" height="275" class="Figure-content"><figcaption class="Figure-caption"><p>Parents said the Common Ground Collective handed out fliers in English and Spanish about the school board election at the Peirce Elementary back-to-school fair. But the QR code directed back to the group’s website, which eventually listed school board endorsements.</p></figcaption><span class="line"></span><div class="Figure-credit"><p>Photos provided by Nicole Granacki</p></div></div> </figure> </div> </div><p>Some of that has gone to one of the more contested school board races in a North Side district that includes Peirce Elementary. The current school board member, Debby Pope, a retired CPS teacher and a CTU stalwart, is running for reelection. Common Ground Collective has endorsed her opponent, Kyna Lenhof, the treasurer of the 40th Ward Democratic Organization, and contributed about $4,000 directly to Lenhof’s campaign. Common Ground Collective’s political groups spent another $37,500 on digital ads supporting Lenhof or opposing Pope.</p><p>Common Ground Collective, like many political groups, also established what is called a social welfare nonprofit, or a 501(c)4.</p><p>Some groups set these up because they legitimately want to promote social welfare, said Aaron McKean, the senior legal counsel at the Washington, D.C.-based Campaign Legal Center, a nonpartisan nonprofit that promotes voter rights.</p><p>But others use this type of nonprofit to hide the identity of donors and obscure political spending, often known as “dark money,” McKean said. Federal law does not require 501(c)4s to reveal their supporters.</p><p>“It’s just evading disclosure,” McKean said. “When it comes to political spending, people have a right to know who is spending to influence their vote, and it’s these kind of poorly worded laws that allow big spenders to find ways to weasel out of that disclosure.”</p><p><a class="Link" href="https://projects.propublica.org/nonprofits/organizations/331552983" target="_blank" ><u>According to its 2025 tax filing</u></a>, Common Ground Collective’s nonprofit had $2.1 million, but it does not show who donated to the organization.</p><p>In a statement, a spokeswoman for Common Ground Collective said the organization has a legitimate social welfare mission and has made donations or hosted tables at school events to “provide backpacks, school supplies or sponsor engagement activities for kids to create fun and strengthen their comfort and excitement for starting the school year.”</p><p>Their website has a <a class="Link" href="https://cgcollective.org/cgc-in-action" target="_blank" ><u>section called “CGC In Action”</u></a> which shows the organization holding a holiday food drive with school board member Carlos Rivas at Nixon Elementary in Hermosa, supporting a community workout event at Juarez High School in Pilsen and handing out turkeys at Michele Clark High School in Austin. In photos of the events, people can be seen holding Common Ground Collective signs.</p><p>Lizzie Turner, the chair of Peirce Elementary’s LSC, said the Common Ground Collective approached their school’s principal, Luis Avila, by touting its social welfare mission.</p><p>In an email to the principal, which was shared with Turner and other LSC members and reviewed by WBEZ, the group described itself as “a 501(c)(4) nonprofit and advocacy organization dedicated to strengthening our CPS schools and working toward a future where every student has access to high-quality public education.”</p><p>In another email shared with the LSC, the Common Ground Collective representative said the group wanted to hire a DJ recommended by Che “Rhymefest” Smith, a current board member of a South Side district. Turner said the first-time principal is new to the school and likely saw Smith’s name as an indication that the offer was okay.</p><p>“He just incorrectly assumed that they were innocent and just wanted to help and were like, ‘Yeah, we'll take a free DJ for our event,’” Turner said.</p><p>Because the DJ’s services were donated, the LSC didn’t have to approve it.</p><p>Turner said that the Peirce LSC and principal already got a stern talking to by CPS officials who wanted to make sure they understood district rules.</p><p>Now Peirce LSC members are asking CPS officials to make sure political advocacy organizations cannot “use partnerships, sponsorships, donations, or other access to CPS schools as a pathway to reach families with candidate advocacy,” according to the letter they sent to the district.</p><p>Smith says he never recommended any DJ to the Common Ground Collective and is unhappy that they dropped his name in that way. Smith, a hip hop artist, says his fame makes him vulnerable to being used.</p><p>In the situation at Peirce, school board member Ellen Rosenfeld also has come under fire because her husband is listed in tax filings as a board member of the nonprofit run by the Common Ground Collective. Peirce LSC members say Rosenfeld should have intervened to stop the group from tabling and handing out fliers on school grounds.</p><p>Peirce LSC members asked CPS to “reinforce clear ethical expectations for Board members and candidates regarding relationships with political organizations, school administrators, vendors, sponsors, and other outside entities during election cycles.”</p><p>Rosenfeld says the tax filing is wrong and that her husband has never been on the board. But she says as long as the endorsements weren’t on the website when the back-to-school fair took place, she sees nothing wrong with what the Common Ground Collective did.</p><p>She said many groups are doing what they can to get their names and their candidates in front of voters.</p><p>“The Chicago Teachers Union is trying to get its name out, SEIU is trying to get its name out,” she said.</p><p>Rosenfeld and Smith are both endorsed by Common Ground Collective, but they are both running unopposed.</p>

Tennessee Williams, 36 at the time, was following up his first Broadway hit “The Glass Menagerie” with a new play, “A Streetcar Named Desire.”</p><div class="Enhancement FormEnhancement" target="_blank" >Privacy Policy</a></p> </div> </form> </bsp-form> </div> </div><p>History tells us that director Elia Kazan gave Brando money to travel to Provincetown, Mass., where Williams was spending the summer, so that the young (and still unknown) actor could read for the part of Stanley Kowalski. Brando pocketed the money and instead hitchhiked with a girlfriend. He arrived three days late but ingratiated himself to the writer by fixing the plumbing and electricity issues plaguing Williams’ bungalow. Then Brando auditioned, got the part, and, some would sincerely say, changed acting forever.</p><p>This play by Gregg Ostrin imagines the rest and turns their first meeting into a concentrated clash of personalities — a playwright both cultured and imperious, an actor both unpretentious and manipulative.</p><div class="RatingCard Enhancement" data-module data-rating="2.5" data-align-center> <div class="RatingCard-title"> “Kowalski” </div> <div class="RatingCard-content"> <span class="RatingCard-star"> <span class="RatingCard-star-full"> <svg class=""> <use xlink:href="#icon-star"></use> </svg> </span> <span class="RatingCard-star-half"> <svg class=""> <use xlink:href="#icon-star"></use> </svg> </span> </span> <span class="RatingCard-star"> <span class="RatingCard-star-full"> <svg class=""> <use xlink:href="#icon-star"></use> </svg> </span> <span class="RatingCard-star-half"> <svg class=""> <use xlink:href="#icon-star"></use> </svg> </span> </span> <span class="RatingCard-star"> <span class="RatingCard-star-full"> <svg class=""> <use xlink:href="#icon-star"></use> </svg> </span> <span class="RatingCard-star-half"> <svg class=""> <use xlink:href="#icon-star"></use> </svg> </span> </span> <span class="RatingCard-star"> <span class="RatingCard-star-full"> <svg class=""> <use xlink:href="#icon-star"></use> </svg> </span> <span class="RatingCard-star-half"> <svg class=""> <use xlink:href="#icon-star"></use> </svg> </span> </span> </div> </div><p></p><div class="RichTextSidebarModule Enhancement" data-module data-align-center><a class="AnchorLink" id="module-010000" name="module-010000"></a> <div class="RichTextModule-items RichTextBody"><b>When</b>: Through October 25th<br><b>Where</b>: Lookingglass Theatre (821 N. Michigan Ave.)<br><b>Tickets</b>: $37–$97<br><b>Info</b>: <a class="Link" href="https://lookingglasstheatre.org" target="_blank" >lookingglasstheatre.org</a><br><b>Running time</b>: 1 hour and 25 minutes with no intermission</div> </div><p>Generally amusing in its lighter parts and strained in its more dramatic ones, Ostrin’s work relies on an audience with a decent amount of “Streetcar” knowledge, but not too much. If you don’t know the play or movie, you won’t get some of the humor. But if you know a good amount, you’ll see the fairly gimmicky concept at work before the plot reveals it, since Williams’ masterpiece also centers on a battle between a cultured and imperious Southerner in Blanche DuBois and an unpretentious, manipulative Stanley.</p><p>“Kowalski” was initially staged off-Broadway but with different leads. At Lookingglass, Johnny Galecki plays Williams, a clear and purposeful departure from his television roles on “The Big Bang Theory” and “Roseanne.” It’s a highly competent performance, but not an inspired one.</p><p>The same is true of Jacob Moskovitz’s (Miles on Amazon Prime’s “Legally Blonde” prequel series “Elle”) turn as Brando. Under Colin Hanlon’s direction, they avoid straight-up impersonations of these famed personalities, but there’s always a sense of performance.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Figure-content"><figcaption class="Figure-caption"><p>In “Kowalski,” the audience watches Galecki perform Williams as the character deploys his wit. And it watches Moskovitz as Brando behaving as Stanley Kowalski.</p></figcaption><span class="line"></span><div class="Figure-credit"><p>Courtesy of Michael Brosilow</p></div></div> </figure> </div> </div><p>What we ultimately get is an overlayered experience. We’re watching Galecki perform Williams as the character deploys his wit alternately to charm and intimidate a young actor he’s clearly intrigued by. And we’re watching Moskovitz as Brando behaving as Stanley Kowalski.</p><p>It reaches peak artifice when the two engage in a power battle over the attentions of Brando’s girlfriend Jo, a role actress Ellie Ricker manages to make likable even though the character is more pawn than person. The other supporting performers here, Alison Cimmet and Reece de Santos, also do solid work with underwritten parts as, respectively, the producer/director Margo Jones and Williams’ boarish (and thus also Stanley-like) boyfriend Pancho.</p><p>At just 85 minutes, the play doesn’t overstay its welcome, but I’m puzzled by the stated Broadway aspirations for this piece, no matter how capable the production. First, it’s simply a modest, even standard piece of writing, showing craft but not especially funny and certainly not moving if it’s supposed to be.</p><p>It also fails to capture what was genuinely special about both of the artists it depicts, how they changed what theater was and could be by reaching for a more truthful portrayal of humanity, somehow both poetic and raw simultaneously. There is simply nothing either poetic or raw about “Kowalski.”</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Enhancement-item" data-crop=""> <figure class="Figure"><a class="AnchorLink" id="image-0e0000" name="image-0e0000"></a> <picture data-crop="medium"> <source type="image/webp" width="490" height="275" Here, from left to right, Johnny Galecki, Alison Cimmet, Ellie Ricker and Jacob Moskovitz make up the cast of “Kowalski.” </p></figcaption><span class="line"></span><div class="Figure-credit"><p>Courtesy of Michael Brosilow</p></div></div> </figure> </div> </div><p>And finally, I question whether we are still in the age — I wish we were! — when Williams and Brando were figures of such public fascination to make fictional portrayals of them a commercial-level draw.</p><p>What we’re primarily left with here is the history, and the nod to artistic greatness.</p><p>I appreciate and encourage the production of new plays. But “Kowalski” — as a type of fan fiction — is exactly the type of work that makes me crave the greatness it refers to. It’s not like we’ve been inundated with productions of “Streetcar” – although Paramount Theatre in Aurora staged a very good one in 2024 – or other of Williams’ works. His full-blooded characters remain figures waiting for further discovery and interpretation.</p><p>Here’s a call for more of the “real” thing, and less of the lore.</p>

entries.title: Bitter fight over Chicago police discipline heads to state Supreme Court
entries.summary: <p>The Illinois Supreme Court is set to hear arguments Thursday on whether disciplinary hearings for Chicago police officers accused of serious misconduct must remain open to the public.</p><p>It marks the latest, and possibly final, chapter in the <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/police-reform/2025/09/16/chicago-police-union-fop-misconduct-discipline" target="_blank" >yearslong legal battle</a> between the city and its largest cop union that has ground Chicago’s police oversight system to a halt.</p><p>There are currently over two dozen officers with pending charges before the Chicago Police Board who have chosen to take their cases to arbitration, leaving them in limbo as they await the court’s ruling.</p><p>“This delay serves no one,” Kyle Cooper, the police board president, said last month. “It leaves serious disciplinary charges unresolved and imposes significant costs on taxpayers.”</p><p>Over the past three years, the case has wound its way from the bargaining table to City Council and now all levels of state court.</p><p>It began in Summer 2023, when an arbitrator overseeing the police union’s collective bargaining negotiations found state law allowed members the <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/city-hall/2023/8/4/23820717/arbitrator-ruling-chicago-police-board-discipline-suspension-firings" target="_blank" >right to “final and binding arbitration,”</a> like other public sector employees.</p><p>City Council voted the decision down twice, handing the issue over to the courts.</p><p>In March 2024, a Cook County judge ruled officers could <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/city-hall/2024/03/21/chicago-cops-serious-discipline-arbitrator-public" target="_blank" >bypass the police board</a> and have their cases heard by an arbitrator, but that hearings could not be held in private. Neither the city nor the Fraternal Order of Police was pleased, prompting a swift appeal.</p><p>Last August, a panel of appellate judges <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/police-reform/2025/08/08/chicago-police-cpd-misconduct-discipline-arbitration-ruling-appellate-court" target="_blank" >upheld the lower court’s ruling</a>, finding that moving hearings behind closed doors would violate public policy, which favors “police accountability and transparency.” The three-judge panel sided with the union by ruling that officers who face firing must still be paid while their cases are pending.</p><p>Still, the police union appealed. In a brief to the state Supreme Court, union attorneys argued the appellate panel had ignored established state law that allows for private arbitration and instead drafted its own rules based on its “own policy preferences.”</p><p>The city responded that moving hearings behind closed doors would break with a decades-old practice and would represent a serious step back in the department’s reform efforts.</p><p>“Transparency, when the most serious police misconduct is on the line, has been crucial in Chicago, where the policing landscape is extraordinarily complex and many residents harbor mistrust towards police,” the city wrote in a brief. “Public hearings build trust and cooperation between CPD and the people it serves”</p><p>Illinois Attorney General Kwame Raoul, whose office filed a lawsuit that spurred a federal consent decree mandating sweeping Chicago police reforms, echoed this warning. </p><p>“Excluding the public from hearings in serious police disciplinary matters would undermine both the Consent Decree’s reforms and public confidence in CPD,” Raoul wrote to the court.</p><p>Regardless of the higher court’s ruling, the police board is asking officers not to seek arbitration.</p><p>Once a decision is released, the city and police union will still have to work to establish an arbitration process, contributing to further delays. But the board is “ready and able to hear disciplinary cases now,” according to Cooper.</p><p>“Officers should not have to spend years with serious charges hanging over them,” he said last month.</p><p>“Alleged victims should not have to wait years for resolution. And Chicago residents should not have to wait years to learn whether serious allegations against a public servant have been proven.”</p><p>But only four of the 31 officers currently facing charges have elected to have their cases heard by the police board.</p><p>The remaining 27 officers have chosen to take their cases to arbitration. Seven of those officers are accused of using deadly force.</p><p>That group includes Officer Eric Stillman, the cop who fatally shot 13-year-old Adam Toledo during a foot chase into an alley in Little Village in March 2021. </p><p>Oral arguments are set to begin at 9 a.m. Thursday and will be streamed on the Illinois Supreme Court’s <a class="Link" href="https://www.illinoiscourts.gov/courts/supreme-court/" target="_blank" >website</a>.</p><div class="RelatedList Enhancement" data-module data-align-center> <div class="RelatedList-title">Related</div> <ul class="RelatedList-items"> <li class="RelatedList-items-item"> <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/police-reform/2025/09/16/chicago-police-union-fop-misconduct-discipline" target="_blank" >Battle over Chicago police disciplinary hearings moves to state Supreme Court</a> </li> <li class="RelatedList-items-item"> <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/police-reform/2025/08/08/chicago-police-cpd-misconduct-discipline-arbitration-ruling-appellate-court" target="_blank" >Chicago cops accused of serious misconduct must face public hearings, appeals court rules</a> </li> <li class="RelatedList-items-item"> <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/city-hall/2024/03/21/chicago-cops-serious-discipline-arbitrator-public" target="_blank" >Chicago cops facing serious discipline can take cases to arbitrator, but judge says hearings should be public</a> </li> </ul> </div> <p></p>

entries.title: Instead of driving to school, more kids are taking the 'bike bus'
entries.summary: <p>It might've looked like a bike parade at first glance.</p><p>It was Friday morning in Ravenswood. A couple dozen children and parents were on bicycles. As they rode through the neighborhood, more kids and parents joined.</p><p>"Big crowd today," one neighbor told the group. She stood in her front yard, waving and photographing the group of cyclists. Parents and kids yelled back, "Good morning!"</p><p>But it wasn't a parade.</p><p>They called it a bike bus — the latest way grade schoolers are getting to class.</p><p>In this case, it was a weekly group ride to Waters Elementary School, 4540 N. Campbell Ave. The group had grown to 100 cyclists by the time they arrived at school just before the 8 a.m. bell.</p><p>Bike buses have grown in popularity since they first appeared in Chicago about four years ago. More than a couple dozen bike buses are now held regularly in the Chicago area.</p><p>The idea behind the bike bus is simple: Once a week, a group of kids and parents bike to school together. Parents typically organize the bike bus and ride as chaperones, blocking drivers at intersections as the group passes. The route is shared in advance. People wait and join along the way.</p><p>"As we ride to school, we get bigger and bigger," Rebecca Resman, a parent who leads a bike bus, told the Sun-Times. "Then we arrive: smiles, joy, all ready to learn."</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Enhancement-item"> <bsp-carousel class="Carousel Enhancement" data-align-center> <a data-src="https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/9240790/2147483647/strip/true/crop/5464x5464+1364+0/resize/300x300!/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2Fda%2Fe4%2Fd003884a47af917b217f3e5887d8%2Fbikebus-260921-020.jpg" data-lazy-load="true" src="data:image/svg+xml;base64,PHN2ZyB4bWxucz0iaHR0cDovL3d3dy53My5vcmcvMjAwMC9zdmciIHZlcnNpb249IjEuMSIgaGVpZ2h0PSIzMDBweCIgd2lkdGg9IjMwMHB4Ij48L3N2Zz4=" > </picture> </span> aria-label="Previous"> <svg class="FlickityCustomNavigation-button-icon"><use xlink:href="#icon-left"></use></svg> </button> <button class="FlickityCustomNavigation-button-next" type="button" aria-label="Next"> <svg class="FlickityCustomNavigation-button-icon"><use xlink:href="#icon-right"></use></svg> </button> </div> </div></div> </bsp-carousel> </div> </div><p>Resman, 44, started one of the city's first bike buses in 2022 at Hamilton Elementary in Lake View for her two children. She tracks bike buses through her group Chicago Family Biking, and estimates there are 30 now operating in the Chicago area.</p><p>People ride for a few reasons. A bike bus provides safety in numbers for parents wary of letting their child bike alone to school. Some people join to socialize. And then there's the excitement.</p><p>"It's a roving party through the neighborhood," Resman said.</p><p>Most bike buses convene once a week. Many pause over the winter. Resman's bike bus typically cancels for bad weather.</p><p>The bike bus concept can be traced to <a class="Link" href="https://citylabbcn.org/the-global-bike-bus-movement/" target="_blank" >Belgium in 1998</a>. But it became popular just as the world emerged from the COVID-19 pandemic. Some Chicago bike bus organizers say they were inspired by Sam Balto, who reportedly <a class="Link" href="https://www.theguardian.com/environment/2025/feb/20/cycling-to-school-almost-became-extinct-until-one-man-revived-the-bike-bus" target="_blank" >organized the first U.S. bike bus in 2022</a> in Portland, Oregon.<b> </b>Balto has said he was inspired by video of a "bicibús" in Barcelona, Spain, the year prior.</p><p>Sten Turpin, 46, said he was inspired by Balto's videos to organize the first bike bus to Waters Elementary in 2023.</p><p>The ride was not an immediate success. For the first couple rides, Turpin, his wife and two children, Felix and Tycho, were the only attendees. More people joined when he settled on the current 2.5-mile route that circles the school.</p><p>"Now we can easily get above 100 riders," Turpin said.</p><p>The point of the bike bus is to encourage and teach kids to ride to school safely, he said.</p><p>"A lot of it has to do with independence and being comfortable riding in the street. It's a low barrier to entry way for kids to start getting that experience," he said.</p><p>Many bike buses are for neighborhood schools, where most students live nearby.</p><p>That’s not the case for Walt Disney Magnet School, in Uptown, where Brad Fisher has been hosting bike buses since 2022. Fisher is the school’s technology coordinator. He has seen ridership grow from less than 10 to upwards of 30.</p><p>At Disney, "kids can come from all over the city. So it's been a challenge to build up. We're starting to see some momentum," Fisher said.</p><p>Bike buses are also about pushing back against the city's car-centric culture.</p><p>Resman pointed out that fewer kids are getting to school on their own.</p><p>In 1969, nearly 50% of children either walked or biked to grade school, according to a national survey. By 2017, the number <a class="Link" href="https://www.pedbikeinfo.org/downloads/PBIC_InfoBrief_NHTS.pdf" target="_blank" >dropped to 11%</a>. Meanwhile, the number of kids driven to school rose from 12% to 50%.</p><p>The bike bus “seems so radical,” she said. “But it's ordinary that these kids are biking to school.”</p><p>She aims to normalize biking.</p><p>“My goal is that we don't need bike buses,” she said.</p><p>But as long as Chicago’s streets are considered dangerous for cyclists and children, parents may have to stick with the safety of the bike bus.</p><p>"I taught my kids to ride a bike [early] and I still get extremely nervous when they go out on their own," Turpin said. "I don't trust drivers. Cars are bigger than they ever been. It's extremely concerning. A lot of it is, we're a big group. We're visible. We're keeping each other safe.”</p>

entries.title: Milwaukee, Detroit or Chicago: Which city has the best encased meats?
entries.summary: <p>Jen Greenwood loves a good encased meat.</p><p>“I joke that I’m a half hot dog. I am not a vegetarian,” she said.</p><p>Greenwood grew up in Evanston, Illinois, spent summers in Michigan and attended college in Milwaukee. She’s eaten more than her fair share of hot dogs and recognizes each region’s unique take on encased meats.</p><p>In Chicago, it’s the Chicago dog; in Milwaukee, the brat; in Detroit, the Coney dog.</p><p>Greenwood wondered: “Why are these hyper-specific encased meats associated so strongly with those three cities?”</p><p>The sausages share an origin story in Germany.</p><p>“Germans, when they came over here, brought their sausage culture with them, and there’s a very heavy German influx into the Americas in the 19th century,” said Bruce Kraig, professor emeritus of history at Roosevelt University and author of “Hot Dog: A Global History.”</p><p>From there, each city made the sausage its own.</p><p>So, who does it best? As much local pride as Chicagoans, Detroiters and Milwaukeeans boast, the answer depends on where you’re from. But Joe Grimm, co-author of “Coney Detroit,” says maybe it’s not about figuring out which is the best.</p><p>“Eating only Chicago dogs or Coneys would not be balanced,” he said. “If you mix it up … the Chicago, Milwaukee, Detroit way, it’s going to be a lot ‘healthier.’”</p><p>Check out each city’s unique encased meat and how its history led to these recipes.</p><p>Disclaimer: These signature sausages can be found all over each city. We only name a few eateries.</p><h3><b>Chicago’s ‘garden on a bun’</b></h3><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Enhancement-item" data-crop=""> <figure class="Figure"><a class="Figure-content"><figcaption class="Figure-caption"><p>A Chicago-style hotdog is sold at Lola’s Coney Island during the Windy City Hot Dog Fest in Portage Park, Saturday, May 31, 2025. </p></figcaption><span class="line"></span><div class="Figure-credit"><p>Pat Nabong/Chicago Sun-Times</p></div></div> </figure> </div> </div><p><b>Origins: </b>Germans brought their pork sausage culture to Chicago in the 1840s and ’50s. Four decades later, Jewish immigrants entered the hot dog business, but they didn’t eat pork.</p><p>“The all-beef hot dog [comes] when Jews took up hot dog stands around Maxwell Street and Roosevelt Road, the epicenter of hot doggery,” Kraig said.</p><p>As more immigrants settled in Chicago, the list of ingredients got longer. For instance, the relish is an old English recipe, while the sport pepper came from Mexico. The “garden on a bun” definitively appeared after World War II, when Americans still recovering from Great Depression scarcity wanted bigger dishes with more fixings.</p><p><b>Ingredients and preparation:</b> All-beef frankfurter with natural casing, boiled or steamed. Served in a steamed poppy-seed bun and topped with yellow mustard, bright green sweet pickle relish, chopped white onions, tomato wedges, a dill pickle spear, pickled sport peppers and a dash of celery salt.</p><p><b>Why it’s the best: </b>The “seven holy condiments.” Not only are they fresh, refreshing and aesthetically pleasing, but they tell a unique story of immigration and culture in Chicago. “You’re looking at Polish, German, Austrian, Mexican, Italian and Greek,” said Chicago food journalist Steve Dolinsky, naming the communities where each ingredient originated.</p><p><b>Where to find it:</b> <a class="Link" href="https://www.wienerscirclechicago.com/" target="_blank" >The Wiener’s Circle</a>, <a class="Link" href="https://superdawg.com/" target="_blank" >Superdawg </a>and <a class="Link" href="https://www.fatsoslaststand.com/" target="_blank" >Fatso’s Last Stand</a> are among the most popular spots. <a class="Link" href="https://www.portillos.com/index.html" target="_blank" >Portillo’s</a> is also a go-to for many Chicagoans.</p><h3><b>A Wisconsin staple</b></h3><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Enhancement-item" data-crop=""> class="Figure-content"><figcaption class="Figure-caption"><p>Bratwurst and fries from Milwaukee Brat House.</p></figcaption><span class="line"></span><div class="Figure-credit"><p>Emily Files/WUWM</p></div></div> </figure> </div> </div><p><b>Origins:</b> Just like beer, brats came to Wisconsin with the massive number of German immigrants in the 1800s. Milwaukee was at one time known as the “German Athens” because of its huge German population.</p><p>In the 1950s, Milwaukee County Stadium <a class="Link" href="https://www.jsonline.com/story/entertainment/dining/2026/07/01/bratwurst-wisconsin-milwaukee-summer/90707920007/" target="_blank" ><u>started selling brats</u></a> at baseball games, and they became a staple ballpark food. The Milwaukee Brewers embraced the brat even more in the 1990s, when the <a class="Link" href="https://www.mlb.com/brewers/fans/mascots/racing-sausages" target="_blank" ><u>Racing Sausages</u></a> came off the scoreboard animation and took to the field as in-game entertainment.</p><p>Brats are ubiquitous at tailgates and can be found on backyard grills across Wisconsin.</p><p><b>Ingredients and preparation:</b> There are lots of variations, but Fritz Usinger, president of Usinger’s Famous Sausage, says they usually sport a combination of ground pork, veal or beef in a natural casing. The meat is mixed with spices like pepper, sage, nutmeg and coriander.</p><p>Toppings vary depending on personal tastes. Lots of Wisconsinites parboil brats in beer and onions before cooking on the grill. Usinger prefers to put them directly on the grill, though beer is still involved.</p><p>“I have what’s called the two-beer method,” he said. “By the time you drink two beers, leisurely, your brat will be done [grilling].”</p><p><b>Why it’s the best: </b>The sausage itself is the star, not the toppings. The flavor of the brat is what makes it special.</p><p><b>Where to find it:</b> <a class="Link" href="https://www.vanguardbar.com/" target="_blank" ><u>The Vanguard</u></a>, <a class="Link" href="https://www.milwaukeebrathouse.com/" target="_blank" ><u>Milwaukee Brat House</u></a> and <a class="Link" href="https://www.vontriers.com/" target="_blank" ><u>Von Trier</u></a> are known for their brats. You can also buy fresh brats from a grocery store (Wisconsin brands include <a class="Link" href="https://www.usinger.com/where-to-buy" target="_blank" ><u>Usinger’s</u></a> and <a class="Link" href="https://johnsonville.com/where-to-buy/" target="_blank" ><u>Johnsonville</u></a>) or specialty butcher and grill it yourself.</p><h3><b>A Detroit delicacy</b></h3><div class="Enhancement" data-lazy-load="true" src="data:image/svg+xml;base64,PHN2ZyB4bWxucz0iaHR0cDovL3d3dy53My5vcmcvMjAwMC9zdmciIHZlcnNpb249IjEuMSIgaGVpZ2h0PSIyNzVweCIgd2lkdGg9IjQ5MHB4Ij48L3N2Zz4=" > </picture> <div class="Figure-content"><figcaption class="Figure-caption"><p>Detroit Coney dog</p></figcaption><span class="line"></span><div class="Figure-credit"><p>Ciaran Carr/ WDET</p></div></div> </figure> </div> </div><p><b>Origins: </b>Local lore says Greek immigrants passing through New York’s Coney Island adopted the name for their dog.</p><p>“Greeks arrived from Greece, mostly at Ellis Island. And on the way, they went through Coney Island, already thinking, ‘How am I going to support myself here?’” Grimm said. “Seeing people eating — not coneys, but eating hot dogs — and [they] said, ‘Okay, these people eat hot dogs. I can do that.’”</p><p>In 1917, Gus Kero opened the famed American Coney Island in Downtown Detroit. Eventually, he brought his brother William to the city to open Lafayette Coney Island next door. Both have remained open ever since.</p><p><b>Ingredients and preparation:  </b>Steamed bun with beef and pork dog in natural casing, topped with an all-meat beanless chili sauce, sprinkled with diced white onions and a drizzle of yellow mustard. The sauce is the key: It’s believed to be a variation of a similar sauce made in Greece, though the exact recipe is a mystery.</p><p><b>Why it’s the best: </b>The bold flavor in the sauce, the snap of the dog and the brightness from the onion and mustard makes the meal most satisfying.</p><p><b>Where to find it: </b>American and Lafayette remain the most widely known locations for the coney dog. The rivalry between the two restaurants is mostly a debate for tourists, though. Ask a native Detroiter and they’ll point you to a number of Coney Island establishments around the city, like <a class="Link" href="https://lgeorges6mile.com/" target="_blank" ><u>L. George’s</u></a>, <a class="Link" href="https://riverviewzorba.com/" target="_blank" ><u>Zorba’s</u></a> and <a class="Link" href="https://nickydsconeyisland.com/" target="_blank" ><u>Nicky D’s</u></a>.</p><p><i>Curious Midwest is a limited series collaboration with Curious City, </i><a class="Link" href="https://www.wuwm.com/bubblertalk" target="_blank" ><i>Bubbler Talk</i></a><i> at WUWM in Milwaukee and </i><a class="Link" href="https://wdet.org/podcasts/curiosid-podcast/" target="_blank" ><i>CuriosiD</i></a><i> at WDET in Detroit.
