entries.title: Legalizing video gambling terminals is a bad bet for Chicago
entries.summary: <p>When the City Council voted to legalize video gambling terminals in bars and restaurants in the 2026 budget, alderpersons put our safety, our tax dollars and our civic reputation in peril.</p><p>Today, we’re seeing the effects. Recently, Bally’s <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/city-hall/2026/09/09/ballys-permanent-casino-river-west-construction-slowdown-video-gambling-terminals-city-council-license-committee" target="_blank" ><u>moved to reset</u></a> the pace of construction on the casino site in River West, citing the legalization of video gambling terminals. Bally’s rightly says the legalization of the terminals stands in direct violation of the historic contract the city of Chicago required of the selected casino operator in 2022. This makes sense. Bally’s committed to making a massive investment in River West and our city, promising and delivering thousands of good, permanent union jobs, not to mention the portion of the proceeds that would fund our police and fire pension liability.</p><p>In exchange, our contract <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/city-hall/2026/08/12/ballys-permanent-casino-river-west-construction-slowdown-council-members-letter" target="_blank" >agreed to not legalize video gambling terminals</a>, which will drastically cut into gaming and pension revenue based on the impact experienced by existing casinos in Illinois historically. Now, the City Council has broken that commitment.</p><div class="RichTextSidebarModule Enhancement" data-module data-align-center><a class="AnchorLink" id="module-2a0000" name="module-2a0000"></a> <div class="RichTextSidebarModule-title">Commentary bug</div> <div class="RichTextModule-items RichTextBody"><h2>Commentary</h2></div> </div><p>Breaking a contract in this way hurts the city’s relationships with other corporations considering doing business here. This also creates uncertainty for surrounding developments to move forward, which contribute to thousands of union jobs, Neighborhood Opportunity Funds, housing and expanding the tax base. Civic leaders and investors see how this has been handled and factor it in when considering whether to open headquarters, make investments or hire workers here.</p><p>As leaders in our own communities, who have been members of the Community Advisory Council since its formation in 2022 and civic organizers for decades, we are alarmed. The advisory council was created to ensure the community’s voice is centered throughout the process of development of the casino, which directly affects our neighbors, citizens and taxpayers. What’s clear to us is our communities have no interest in undermining our city’s safety and financial security to elevate video gambling terminals. We’ve had direct conversations with constituents, our residents, our taxpayers, including among white, Black and Latino Chicagoans. They do not want video gambling terminals or any of the negative impacts associated with them; they have too many financial and public health concerns already.</p><p>Illinois casinos have <a class="Link" href="https://www.chicagobusiness.com/real-estate/commercial/ccb-ballys-chicago-casino-delay-video-gambling-20260825/" target="_blank" ><u>seen a nearly 40% reduction</u></a> in gaming revenue directly attributed to video gambling terminals. Why are we not talking about this? This means losing nearly $100 million in tax revenue for the city’s police and firefighters pension funds. It’s a terrible deal for taxpayers and even worse for our first responders. Imagine cutting a deal to, at best break even, while eliminating good-paying union jobs earmarked for Chicagoans!</p><p>Did the City Council at least make a related public safety plan to make sure we are equipped to handle the <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/the-watchdogs/2026/01/20/video-gambling-establishments-spike-burglaries-illinois-gaming-board-chicago-suburbs" target="_blank" ><u>spike in crime</u></a> that happens in neighborhoods surrounding establishments with video gambling termnals? Nope, they didn’t do that, either. Casinos have an intense security presence at a single location. But video gambling terminals lack the same strong, embedded security measures. All we need to do is look to south suburban <a class="Link" href="https://wgntv.com/news/another-arrest-made-in-oak-lawn-video-gaming-terminal-theft-investigation/" target="_blank" ><u>Oak Lawn</u></a> to see what is in store for our neighborhoods. There, they’ve seen a rash of video gambling terminal-related burglaries — and they’ve sounded the alarm about the lack of resources to combat it.</p><p>As Oak Lawn Village Manager Tom Phelan said during a village board meeting earlier this year, “Someone’s going to get killed. Whether it be police, whether it be, God help us if it’s just innocent victims.”</p><p>There’s still time for the alderpersons to fix their mistake. They should reverse this ill-advised video gambling terminal legalization before the machines start showing up all over town.</p><p><i>John Bosca is a community leader and organizer for Neighbors of River West, chair of the Casino Advisory Council, and a commercial real estate professional with 30-plus years of experience in the Chicago area.</i></p><p><i>Julie Darling is a Chicago-born community advocate, nonprofit leader, and experiential marketing professional with more than 25 years of experience in the nonprofit world.</i></p><div class="RichTextSidebarModule Enhancement" data-module data-align-center><a class="AnchorLink" id="module-180000" name="module-180000"></a> <div class="RichTextModule-items RichTextBody">Send letters to <a class="Link" href="mailto:letters@suntimes.com" target="_blank" >letters@suntimes.com</a>. More about <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/submitting-opinion-and-letters" >how to submit here</a>.</div> </div><p></p>

entries.title: Thief made off with 8 e-scooters by removing ignitions in several North Side neighborhoods
entries.summary: <p>Chicago police are looking for a thief who has swiped at least eight e-scooters by removing their ignitions since June on the North Side.</p><p>The robber is described as a white man in his 50s wearing a white shirt, blue shorts and a fanny pack and he targeted scooters in the Bucktown, Lake View East, Uptown, Roscoe Village and Lincoln Square neighborhoods, police said.</p><p>In each of the thefts, he removed the ignition of the scooters to bypass the key start function, officials said.</p><p>The thefts occurred at the following times and locations: <br></p><ul class="rte2-style-ul" id="rte-a69f35e2-b74e-11f1-84ce-1fb8b07065a3" data-pm-slice="3 1 []"><li>1800 block of West Webster Avenue on Sept. 13, 2026 at 7:30 p.m.</li><li>4700 block of North Western Avenue on Aug. 22, 2026 at 7:00 p.m.</li><li>4600 block of North Western Avenue on Aug. 18, 2026 at 6:00 p.m.</li><li>1900 block of West Roscoe Street on July 21, 2026 at 3:00 p.m.</li><li>600 block of West Briar Place on July 8, 2026 at 2:00 p.m.</li><li>3500 block of North Lake Shore Drive on June 30, 2026 at 6:30 p.m.</li><li>4100 block of North Sheridan Road on June 21, 2026 at 12:00 p.m.</li><li>700 block of West Brompton Avenue on June 9, 2026 at 1:00 p.m.</li></ul><p>Anyone with information should call Area 3 detectives, 312-744-8263 or Area 5 detectives at 312-746-7394. entries.title: 'Broadview Six' judge to hold hearing next week as she weighs consequences of feds' misconduct
entries.summary: <p>The judge who discovered<b> </b>apparent misconduct by prosecutors<b> </b>in the "Broadview Six" conspiracy case has scheduled a hearing next week<b> </b>to help her decide what to do about the discovery that shook the Dirksen Federal Courthouse this summer.</p><p>U.S. District Judge April Perry said she will hear arguments Oct. 1 over whether to appoint an independent special counsel<b> </b>to investigate U.S. Attorney Andrew Boutros and others for criminal contempt, among other possible sanctions. She revealed her plans in an order on the court docket Wednesday.</p><p>It’s the most substantive step from Perry in months, coming after she revealed alleged wrongdoing by the feds.<b> </b>She told lawyers May 21 that, “although I am not going to prejudge the issue without a hearing, I will say that I was incredibly shocked.”</p><div class="RelatedList Enhancement" data-module data-align-center> <div class="RelatedList-title">Related</div> <ul class="RelatedList-items"> <li class="RelatedList-items-item"> <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/crime/2026/08/17/broadview-six-judge-april-perry-trump-vance" >‘Broadview 6' judge has to decide whether to hold prosecutors accountable after exposing misconduct</a> </li> </ul> </div> <p>Now, the time for such a hearing has apparently come.</p><p>News of the hearing follows months of back-and-forth in court filings, as defense attorneys and prosecutors argued over what should happen next.</p><p>The <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/crime/2026/06/27/broadview-six-boutros-chicago" target="_blank" >“Broadview Six” </a>revelations triggered a credibility crisis for Boutros unlike any faced by his recent predecessors. More than 100 former federal prosecutors<b> </b>called out a <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/immigration/2026/06/08/broadview-six-andrew-boutros-federal-prosecutor-justice-department-doj" >“failure of leadership”</a><b> </b>in his office. A chorus of local Democratic elected officials called for his resignation. And the long-held assumption that judges could take the feds at their word began to crumble.</p><p>Boutros responded by announcing a set of<b> </b>“sweeping” reforms,”<b> </b>including a review of nearly <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/crime/2026/06/22/broadview-six-damage-spreads-boutros-drops-more-charges-details-ongoing-review" target="_blank" >20 years of work </a>by the veteran prosecutor primarily accused of mishandling the “Broadview Six” case, Assistant U.S. Attorney Sheri<b> </b>Mecklenburg. </p><p>The<b> </b>prosecution<b> </b>revolved around an Operation Midway Blitz protest<b> </b>on Sept. 26, 2025. Prosecutors alleged that a crowd pushed and damaged a federal agent’s SUV. But from that crowd, only six were charged with conspiring<b> </b>to impede a federal agent. Most of the defendants were involved in local Democratic politics.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Enhancement-item" data-crop=""> <figure class="Figure"><a data-lazy-load="true" src="data:image/svg+xml;base64,PHN2ZyB4bWxucz0iaHR0cDovL3d3dy53My5vcmcvMjAwMC9zdmciIHZlcnNpb249IjEuMSIgaGVpZ2h0PSIyNzVweCIgd2lkdGg9IjQ5MHB4Ij48L3N2Zz4=" > </picture> <div class="Figure-content"><figcaption class="Figure-caption"><p>A crowd surrounds a federal agent’s vehicle outside the U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement facility in Broadview on Sept. 26, 2025.</p></figcaption><span class="line"></span><div class="Figure-credit"><p>Anthony Vazquez/Sun-Times</p></div></div> </figure> </div> </div><p>Those charged were then-congressional candidate Kat Abughazaleh, Oak Park village trustee Brian Straw, then-Cook County Board candidate Catherine “Cat” Sharp, 45th Ward Democratic committeeperson Michael Rabbitt, musician<b> </b>Joselyn Walsh and Abughazaleh campaign worker Andre Martin.</p><p>The one-year anniversary of the protest is Saturday.</p><p>The feds <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/immigration/2026/03/12/chicago-midway-blitz-immigration-trump-kat-abughazaleh-sharp-joselyn-walsh-broadview-six" target="_blank" >dropped charges</a> against Walsh and Sharp in March. Then, on the eve of trial in late May, defense attorneys convinced Perry to review unredacted transcripts of grand jury proceedings in the case. The feds had previously given her redacted versions.</p><p>Perry later said she'd found three types of prosecutorial misconduct in the unredacted transcripts. Mecklenburg is accused of speaking with grand jurors outside the grand jury room and of excusing grand jurors who didn’t agree with the feds’ case.</p><p>The transcripts, which have since been made public, show Mecklenburg excused a grand juror who called the “Broadview Six” case a <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/immigration/2026/06/09/broadview-six-grand-jury-midway-blitz-boutros-trump" target="_blank" >“crock of s---.”</a></p><div class="RelatedList Enhancement" data-module data-align-center> <div class="RelatedList-title">Related</div> <ul class="RelatedList-items"> <li class="RelatedList-items-item"> <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/crime/2026/06/27/broadview-six-boutros-chicago" >What to know about the ‘Broadview Six’ scandal rocking Chicago’s federal courthouse</a> </li> </ul> </div> <p>The prosecutor is also accused of a forbidden practice known as “vouching.” It occurs when prosecutors put their personal credibility on the line to support criminal charges. Grand jurors are expected to hand up indictments based on evidence, not the goodwill of a prosecutor who already has the upper hand in the grand jury room.</p><p>One key example of alleged vouching came Oct. 9, 2025, when Mecklenburg told grand jurors “I don’t charge people unless I’m absolutely sure.”</p><p>Boutros<b> </b>acknowledged<b> </b>this summer<b> </b>that he’d been emailed<b> </b>a transcript<b> </b>of that proceeding last fall, but he said he didn’t remember reading it. He told Perry in May that he’d learned of the vouching in late April.</p><p>Perry also mentioned a fourth concern: The alleged misconduct had been redacted out of the transcripts initially given to her by the feds. She called that “the most problematic”<b> </b>issue of all.</p><p>Four weeks after Perry revealed what she’d found, the former defendants<b> </b>asked Perry<b> </b>to take the extraordinary step of <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/immigration/2026/06/17/broadview-6-want-special-counsel-to-probe-boutros-office-trumps-justice-department-for-criminal-contempt" target="_blank" >appointing a special counsel</a><b> </b>to investigate Boutros and other Justice Department officials for criminal contempt.</p><p>Boutros has since acknowledged <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/crime/2026/08/05/boutros-broadview-six-perry" target="_blank" >“mistakes were made.”</a> But he's said his reforms are meant to prevent them from happening again. He noted his office<b> </b>is not accused of explicitly violating any order from Perry regarding the grand jury transcripts, but he admitted the “better course” would have been to give her unredacted copies of the grand jury transcripts in the first place.</p>

concerns</b>: Parents and other members of a Local School Council are asking Chicago Public Schools to sanction Common Ground Collective, an organization they say violated CPS' rules by electioneering at a back-to-school festival on school grounds. A nonprofit affiliated with the group, which is heavily funded by billionaire Michael Sacks and opposes the Chicago Teachers Union, paid for the DJ and handed out fliers with QR codes directing to endorsements.</p><p><b>Key context</b>: The controversy illustrates how schools are navigating ethically thorny situations ahead of the Nov. 3 election, when <a class="Link" href="https://newsletters.suntimes.com/t/t-l-ydjjoyk-l-u/" target="_blank" >voters will elect all 21 members of the school board for the first time</a>. Some see this election as a test of whether anyone can wrest control from the powerful CTU and Mayor Brandon Johnson, a CTU ally.</p><p><b>At issue</b>: As of Tuesday, $3.3 million has poured into the coffers of school board candidates. On top of that, political groups are spending on ads about candidates. That's a result of "Deb’s Law," inspired by Deb Robertson, who has an aggressive form of cancer and spent years advocating for the right to end her life with medication, should she choose to do so. Gov. JB Pritzker signed the bill into law last year, saying he'd been moved by stories of people or their loved ones who suffered from a terminal illness.</p><p><b>What to know:</b> The measure has become a lightning rod for some religious and disability rights groups who worry it could lead to abuse, but despite court challenges, the law still stands. kids are taking the ‘bike bus’</a></h3><p></p><h5>Reporting by <a class="Link" href="https://newsletters.suntimes.com/t/t-l-ydjjoyk-l-td/" target="_blank" >David Struett</a></h5><p>It might've looked like a bike parade at first glance. It was Friday morning in Ravenswood, and a couple dozen children and parents were on bicycles. As they rode through the neighborhood, more kids and parents joined.</p><p>"Big crowd today," one neighbor told the group. She stood in her front yard, waving and photographing the group of cyclists. Parents and kids yelled back, "Good morning!"</p><p>But it wasn't a parade. They called it a bike bus. Since they first appeared in Chicago about four years ago, bike buses — groups of kids and parents bicycling to school — have been growing in popularity.</p><p>Parents typically organize the bike bus and ride as chaperones, blocking drivers at intersections as the group passes.</p><p>People ride for a few reasons. A bike bus provides safety in numbers for parents wary of letting their child bike alone to school. Some people join to socialize. And then there's the excitement. Bike buses are also about pushing back against the city's car-centric culture.</p><p>"A lot of it is, we're a big group. We’re visible. We're keeping each other safe," one bike bus parent said.</p><p><a class="Link" href="https://newsletters.suntimes.com/t/t-l-ydjjoyk-l-th/" target="_blank" ><b>READ MORE</b></a></p><hr><p></p><h4>YOUR DAILY QUESTION ☕️</h4><p><b>Where is your favorite place to ride a bicycle in the Chicago area? entries.title: Third person charged with murder of man pushed from moving Red Line train
entries.summary: <p>An 18-year-old Morgan Park neighborhood man will appear in court Wednesday, marking the third suspect charged in homicide of Kyle Bickham, who was pushed off of a Red Line train Sept. 7 near the 69th Street Station.</p><p>Christian McBounds, 18, was charged with one count of first-degree murder, two additional murder counts, one count of aggravated battery of a transit employee and one count of mob action, Chicago police said. </p><p>McBounds, of Morgan Park, was expected to appear for a court hearing Wednesday. </p><p>Katlar Parchman, 19, has <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/crime/2026/09/19/second-person-charged-with-murder-after-man-shoved-from-moving-red-line-train" target="_blank" >already been charged</a> with the murder and is the second person to be detained after a 15-year-old girl was charged last week, according to police.</p><p>Parchman, of West Garfield Park, was arrested in the 200 block of North Keeler Avenue after investigators identified her as one of the people who allegedly pushed Bickham from a moving train Sept. 7 near the 69th Street station, police said. Parchman was ordered detained until trial during her first court appearance on Saturday.</p><p>On the day he was killed, a fight broke out on the train between Bickham and Parchman, the teen-aged girl and two males who haven’t been charged, according to a statement from Cook County prosecutors. Police originally reported that three people attacked Bickham.</p><p>Bickham and the teen girl started arguing, and at one point, Bickham allegedly spit at the girl and hit Parchman, according to CTA surveillance footage reviewed by prosecutors. Soon after, all four attackers started repeatedly punching Bickham. One of the males choked him, while the other male pulled the emergency lever for one of the train’s sliding doors as it was moving.</p><p>The 15-year-old girl grabbed Bickham by his head and shoulders and, with the help of one of the males, threw him out of the moving train, according to prosecutors. Bickham was hit by a train traveling in the other direction.</p><p>Witnesses allegedly heard Parchman say, “He shouldn’t have bothered us.”</p>

entries.title: Bears report: Good and bad in non-quarterback injury updates ahead of Eagles game
entries.summary: <p>What's happening Wednesday at Halas Hall:</p><p><b>QB issues</b><br>Starting quarterback Caleb Williams (hamstring) won't practice, and backup Tyson Bagent (concussion) isn't even in the building. Third-stringer Case Keenum, 38, will run the first-team offense with practice-squad quarterback Miller Moss behind him.</p><p><b>Stevenson likely out</b><br><a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/bears" target="_blank" >Bears</a> cornerback Tyrique Stevenson suffered a hamstring injury against the Vikings, and coach <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/bears/2026/09/11/as-engineer-and-artist-blend-styles-bears-ben-johnson-gets-goosebumps-about-future-with-caleb-williams" >Ben Johnson</a> said he’s “week-to-week,” indicating an unlikelihood of having him against the Eagles on Monday.</p><p><b>Help on the way?</b><br>Bears left tackle Ozzy Trapilo was scheduled to go through his first full practice in pads, Johnson said; they aren’t required to specify participation until Thursday. It would be his second full practice as the team looks to get him back in the starting lineup.</p><p><b>Turner time</b><br>Bears 2025 second-round pick Shemar Turner barely played as a rookie and tore his ACL midseason, keeping him out all of training camp, but the team opened the practice window for him and linebacker Noah Sewell to progress toward coming off the physically-unable-to-perform list as early as Week 5 against the Packers.</p><p><b>Short conversation</b><br>Johnson’s <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/bears/2026/08/15/bears-coach-ben-johnson-expects-de-montez-sweat-lt-braxton-jones-soon-but-cb-kyler-gordon-still-unknown" >least favorite subject</a> came up before practice: Are there any indications that nickel cornerback Kyler Gordon’s health is improving? He said only, “I’ve not nothing to add there,” then looked for the next question.</p>

entries.title: Mundelein coach and teacher accused of recording student exercising and stretching
entries.summary: <p>A Mundelein coach and teacher was charged with video recording a student while they were exercising and stretching.</p><p>Dagoberto Diaz, 48, was charged with felony unauthorized video recording of a juvenile, the Mundelein police department said. </p><p>On Aug. 18, police were alerted by the Mundelein School District 75 and 120 administrations after a student reported Diaz allegedly holding a phone that flashed while she did jumping and stretching exercises, police said. </p><p>Diaz, who is a teacher at Carl Sandburg Middle School and Mundelein High School junior varsity volleyball coach, had his phone legally seized and several images and videos were found that "corroborated the student’s initial suspicion," police said. </p><p>Diaz was taken into custody at a family member's home Sept. 22 and was taken to the Lake County Jail pending a first appearance hearing.</p>

entries.title: Case Keenum the only active Bears QB to practice Wednesday
entries.summary: <p>Third-stringer Case Keenum is the only <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/bears" target="_blank" >Bears </a>quarterback on the active roster who will practice Wednesday, coach Ben Johnson said.</p><p>Still, he said, he's "not sure who the starter's going to be" Monday night against the Eagles. </p><p>Second-stringer <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/bears/2026/09/22/bears-qb-tyson-bagent-concussion-case-keenum" target="_blank" >Tyson Bagent </a>was placed in the NFL's concussion protocol after replacing starter Caleb Williams for the last half of the fourth quarter in Sunday's 9-3 home loss to the Eagles. Bagent was not at Halas Hall on Wednesday as part of that protocol.</p><p>Johnson learned about Bagent going into protocol when he received a text Tuesday morning. He presumes, but does not know for sure, that Bagent was injured when he was hit by outside linebacker Andrew Van Ginkel on third down, two plays after he replaced Williams.</p><p>Williams, who pulled his hamstring, won't practice all week. Johnson has yet to officially rule him out for Monday night's game, but his participation seems unlikely.</p><p>Johnson said having to deal with the injury was "foreign" to Williams, who until Sunday had yet to miss a significant snap as a pro.</p><p>"I know he's an antsy individual," Johnson said. "He's a competitor. He wants to be out there on the grass going full speed. So it is a little bit more challenging to hold a guy back like that. But if you could build a player, that's what you'd want him to be."</p><p>Keenum, 38, has started 66 career games but hasn't thrown a pass in a regular season game since 2023. Keenan was sharp this preseason, albeit against backups. posting a 107.7 passer rating and going 25-for-40 for 354 yards and two touchdowns.</p><p>Johnson pointed to Keenum's college success Wednesday. When he left Houston, he was the leading passer in NCAA history with both 19,217 yards and 155 touchdowns.</p><p>"He's been a baller from the day he was born ..." Johnson said. "He's got that way about him. He's got a knack. His teammates gravitate to him. I think that's a good starting [point for a quarterback. And of course he's up there in years a little bit, but that experience has really paid off for him. He sees the game the same way we do. I think he accelerates through his progressions because he's seen so many things over the course of his time. He's been in so many different offenses. So in a lot of ways, he might be a step slower than he was when he first entered the league, and yet his mind is going so fast it helps catch him on up. And he's playing as good of football as he probably has his entire career, is what he'd tell you."</p><p>Rookie Miller Moss, who is on the practice squad, would serve as the second-stringer in practice and Monday's game if the Williams and Bagent can't go.</p>

entries.title: Chicago extends Divvy contract with changes to parking and new bike model coming
entries.summary: <p>The City of Chicago is extending its contract with Divvy as the network of rentable bikes, e-bikes and scooters plans to bring changes to its system, including discounted pricing on the South and West sides and updates to its equipment.</p><p>Divvy, operated by Lyft, has locked in business with the city until 2033, the city announced Wednesday.</p><p>The bikes originally launched in 2013 and use has steadily grown since then, with the company reporting 6.8 million rides last year.</p><p>“As we continue to make equitable investments to build safer streets throughout our neighborhoods, we are committed to keeping transportation affordable and reliable while modernizing the system to provide residents and visitors with a safe, accessible, and dependable way to get where they need to go,” Mayor Brandon Johnson said in a news release.</p><p>Divvy will introduce a 50% discount on non-member rides that start or end on the South and West Sides, a plan that Ald. Daniel La Spata (1st) said “is about making sure the system continues to work for more people in more neighborhoods.”</p><p>The company is launching other cost-saving measures for customers, too. The price for annual memberships will be frozen, and scooter pricing will also be reduced, the release said. The company will implement a cap on price increases throughout the duration of the contract.</p><p>Thousands more e-bikes and scooters will be added under the new contract and a new model of the classic bike will be introduced, which adds a cable lock and rear wheel immobilizers.</p><p>Divvy also aims to simplify parking by adding overflow and “virtual stations,” or public bike racks where Divvy bikes and scooters can be kept, allowing users to end trips even when the Divvy stations are full.</p><p>The contract extension still needs to be approved by the City Council.</p><p>Divvy is planning to expand its “Core Area,” the high-use locations in the city where the company will add more classic bikes, e-bikes, scooters and station docks. More than 100 union jobs will be added with this part of the contract, the release said.</p>

entries.title: Ciudadano estadounidense de Evanston resulta herido en un enfrentamiento con ICE el domingo
entries.summary: <p>La policía de Evanston, un suburbio del norte, investiga un incidente ocurrido el domingo por la mañana que involucró a un residente, ciudadano estadounidense, y a agentes del Servicio de Inmigración y Control de Aduanas (ICE).</p><p>El incidente ocurrió cerca de Howard Street y Dodge Avenue alrededor de las 9:49 a.m. La policía fue enviada al lugar luego de que una persona desconocida llamara para reportar que escuchó a dos hombres discutiendo y a alguien decir que un individuo sería puesto bajo custodia.</p><p>Cuando llegó la Policía de Evanston, encontró a un hombre en el suelo con varias personas ayudándolo. Un <a class="Link" href="https://www.facebook.com/reel/1805994363913682" target="_blank" >video</a> publicado en Facebook muestra al hombre en el suelo con dos agentes intentando detenerlo, a pesar de que él insistía en que era ciudadano estadounidense.</p><div class="RichTextSidebarModule Enhancement" data-module data-align-center><a class="AnchorLink" id="module-940000" name="module-940000"></a> <div class="RichTextModule-items RichTextBody"><h3>La Voz Chicago WhatsApp</h3>Encuentra más noticias en nuestro canal de WhatsApp. <a class="Link" href="https://www.whatsapp.com/channel/0029Vb0XT1XCHDylm3rCs40P" target="_blank" ><b>Síguenos.</b></a></div> </div><p>En el video se le escucha gritarles a los agentes mientras un transeúnte graba.</p><p>El video, de más de tres minutos, muestra a los dos agentes soltando al hombre y abandonando el lugar en vehículos separados, mientras el sujeto seguía en el suelo.</p><p>El hombre les dijo a los agentes que tenía lesiones en el cuello, la cabeza y los dientes.</p><p>Los agentes federales dijeron a la Policía de Evanston que intentaron identificar a una persona que se parecía a alguien que estaban buscando. Un agente dijo a la policía que el individuo se negó a mostrar identificación, fue detenido para tomarle huellas dactilares y se resistió al arresto.</p><p>Más tarde, los agentes determinaron que no era la persona que buscaban y supieron que era ciudadano estadounidense. Fue liberado.</p><p>El agente también dijo que los agentes federales abandonaron el área después de que empezaron a reunirse manifestantes, porque temían ser atacados.</p><p>Más tarde, los agentes se comunicaron con el individuo detenido, un residente adulto de Evanston, en un hospital local.</p><p>"Esto es algo que no debería estar pasando en mi ciudad. No debería estar pasando en las calles de Evanston, pero no debería estar pasando en ninguna ciudad del país", dijo Nathan Ryan, de Sanctuary Evanston, un grupo local de respuesta rápida.</p><p>Sanctuary Evanston y la Coalición por los Derechos de los Inmigrantes y Refugiados de Illinois (ICIRR) emitieron una declaración conjunta en la que condenaron la violencia y pidieron a las autoridades electas investigar el incidente.</p><p>"Que agentes federales agredan a personas en las calles no hace nuestra comunidad más segura para nadie. Sin importar su estatus, todos y cada uno de nuestros vecinos merecen dignidad y seguridad", dijeron ambos grupos.</p><p>El Departamento de Seguridad Nacional de Estados Unidos (DHS) y ICE no respondieron de inmediato a una solicitud de comentarios. La Policía de Evanston continúa investigando el incidente, que ocurre en un momento de mayor interacción con agentes federales de inmigración.</p><p>El domingo en Austin, Texas, un agente de ICE le disparó a un hombre durante una parada de tránsito y luego manifestantes se reunieron contra ICE cerca de la escena durante horas, <a class="Link" href="https://apnews.com/article/austin-texas-ice-shooting-driver-wilber-perez-ebdb9d481d28e322f62c15f1076f3c18" target="_blank" >según The Associated Press</a>.</p><p>El jefe de la Policía de Austin dijo que el hombre baleado estaba en condición grave pero estable en un hospital el domingo por la tarde. Una abogada de inmigración lo identificó como Wilber Rafael Garces Pérez, un venezolano de 28 años. Garcas Pérez estaba haciendo una entrega de comida de DoorDash cuando le dispararon.</p><p>Según The Associated Press, DHS dijo que el hombre está bajo custodia mientras espera ser deportado del país.</p><p>Más cerca de casa, agentes federales usaron gas pimienta contra manifestantes afuera de la instalación de ICE en Broadview el sábado, mientras los manifestantes bloqueaban una entrada vehicular al centro, según Block Club Chicago.</p><p>"Esto no se trata de hacer cumplir las leyes migratorias. Se trata de violencia", dijo Ryan. "Lo único que creo que es más aterrador que ver a agentes federales golpear a personas en la calle es ver a agentes federales golpear a personas en la calle sin consecuencias ni rendición de cuentas".</p><p><i>Michael Puente es reportero y presentador de WBEZ. Contáctalo en mpuente@wbez.org. </i></p><p><i>Traducido con una herramienta de inteligencia artificial (IA) y editado por los seres humanos de</i> <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/la-voz" target="_blank" ><i>La Voz Chicago</i></a><br></p>

entries.title: Eight changes to the local high school basketball landscape
entries.summary: <p>There have been many changes in high school basketball — some big, some small — in the last several years. Here is a look at eight of them:</p><h3>Shot clock</h3><p>While nearly every major basketball event in the state — from holiday tournaments to high-profile shootouts — have used the 35-second shot clock for the last couple of years, it becomes official in the 2026-27 season. That includes, for the first time, in the IHSA state tournament.</p><h3>Transfers</h3><p>There have been transfers, including high-profile ones, dating back decades. But players today are transferring in numbers never seen before.</p><h3>Coaching hires</h3><p>There was once an emphasis — even some pressure — for a high school, especially one that made athletics a priority, to land a hotshot coaching candidate. Thanks to many factors, that isn’t the case anymore.</p><h3>Media coverage</h3><p>Local newspapers shined a bright spotlight on high school basketball for decades. Be it staff writers assigned to prep sports or ‘‘stringers’’ freelancing, dozens of games were covered on a Friday night.</p><p>Now, mostly because of cuts in staff throughout the newspaper industry, the attention on the sport has dwindled greatly in the last 15 to 20 years.</p><p>But if tweets and 30-second highlights from a game on social media do it for you, you’re in the right era.</p><h3>Public League basketball</h3><p>If someone had not laid eyes on high school basketball in the city for 15 or 20 years and came back this year, it might be unrecognizable to them.</p><p>There hasn’t been a Public League team in a big-school (Class 3A or 4A) title game in the last three seasons. This comes after 21 city teams — including 15 state champions — competed in IHSA title games in the previous 16 seasons.</p><p>And you can count the Division I prospects from the Public League in an individual class on one hand. That’s a far cry from when there used to be three or four in a single program not too long ago.</p><h3>Private-school basketball</h3><p>The script has been flipped.</p><p>While Public League basketball has faltered in recent years, the presence of private schools in the postseason has been elevated.</p><p>Nine private schools have played in a big-school (Class 3A or 4A) championship game since 2022, and five have won a state title. In the previous 50 years, a private school playing in a state-championship game was almost unheard of.</p><h3>Prep schools raiding the state</h3><p>It wasn’t that long ago when prep schools weren’t a thing. Remember Anthony Davis, Jabari Parker, Jahlil Okafor, EJ Liddell, Jalen Brunson, Tyler Ulis and more? They all stayed in Illinois, played and left a legacy and at their respective high schools.</p><p>Prep schools have been hitting Illinois hard in recent years. And the top players have listened and departed.</p><h3>College recruiting</h3><p>Twelve years ago, there were 50-plus Division I college players from Illinois. While it wasn’t one of the all-time great classes, it was still a strong one.</p><p>This season? The Class of 2027 will be lucky to inch past 15 Division I players, by far the lowest number in state history. The classes of 2025, 2024 and 2023 produced only 25, 29 and 27 Division I players, respectively.</p><p>The combination of the Public League’s talent drying up, the overall talent in the state being down, players leaving the state and what has happened in college basketball with the transfer portal have led to this shift.</p>

entries.title: Mayoral allies stall measure that would raise the bar on City Hall's ability to take on more debt
entries.summary: <p>Forty percent of Chicago’s operating budget is gobbled up by pension and debt payments — which is why opposition aldepersons want to make it tougher for Mayor Brandon Johnson or his successor to add to that mountain of debt.</p><p>But they'll have to wait a while longer.</p><p>Mayoral allies temporarily derailed an ordinance at Wednesday's City Council meeting <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/city-hall/2026/09/14/city-council-finance-committee-borrowing-threshold-marty-quinn" >that would require </a>future borrowing to be approved by a three-fifths vote. That’s 30 votes instead of the current benchmark of 26.</p><p>Retiring Ald. Marty Quinn (13th) is championing the reform, in what amounts to the latest show of force by the City Council majority that rejected Johnson’s corporate head tax. </p><p>But Budget Committee Chair Jason Ervin (28th), the mayor’s most powerful political ally, used a parliamentary maneuver to delay the final vote for at least one meeting. If 26 votes is "enough to pass any and every" other piece of legislation, Ervin said it makes no sense to "allow a minority of members to effectively hold everybody hostage." </p><p>“Why now? We need to look at the optics of how this will be perceived — especially in minority communities, as to what’s being done to whom, by whom," Ervin told his colleagues at last week's Finance Committee meeting.</p><p>Senior mayoral adviser Jason Lee has similarly argued that allowing a minority to block “bond ordinances for critical infrastructure for whatever reason” would only “lead to gridlock and potentially harmful delays on critical investments that the city needs to make to preserve” roads, bridges and other aging infrastructure.</p><p></p><p>Civic Federation President Joe Ferguson said earlier this month that raising the bar for issuing new city debt “isn’t a political thing. This is math.” <br>According to the Civic Federation, the city’s outstanding net debt rose by 32.8%, from $22 billion to $29.2 billion, between 2014 and 2023 — an amount driven by increased O’Hare Airport debt that was retired by airline revenue.</p><p></p><p></p><p>Last year, the Council almost blocked an <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/city-hall/2025/02/18/830-million-bond-issue-city-borrowing-costs-backloaded-repayment-schedule" target="_blank" >$830 million general obligation bond issue</a> that included a back-loaded repayment schedule that raised the overall price tag to $2 billion. Johnson’s 26-23 victory was secured only after the mayor had to cast the third tie-breaking vote of his tenure. </p><p></p><p></p><h3>Johnson’s data centers moratorium bid</h3><p>Johnson followed through on his <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/city-hall/2026/08/11/mayor-brandon-johnson-chicago-moratorium-data-centers-new-regulations" >promise to propose a one-year moratorium</a> on new or expanded data centers until permanent regulations are established to mitigate their impact on the power grid, the water supply and the environment.</p><div class="Enhancement" The measure was referred to the Rules Committee in an attempt to slow it down.</p><p>Villegas said a moratorium should be confined to what he called “hyper-scalers.” That refers to new and expanded data centers with more than 500,000 square feet of space — not the 1,000-square-foot and “20% of total enclosed floor space” cut-off that Johnson proposed.</p><p>“The city needs revenue and we have an opportunity to do it responsibly. I’m not saying we put data centers everywhere. But there’s vacant buildings right now. Class C buildings that are not going to get new tenants and they have power. So why don’t we capitalize on that?” Villegas said.</p><p>“We don’t need these large farms… taking up acres of land when we can do vertical, urban edge computing, repurpose empty commercial buildings, collect property tax revenue and collect personal property lease tax revenue in an industry where we’re perfectly situated given the fiber and density in our city.”</p><p>Villegas said Northwestern Memorial Hospital and Chicago's most prestigious universities all have data centers.</p><p>"Are you going to ban those? You need data centers,” he said. “This is political because it’s popular. And unfortunately, the mayor is in a tight race and he sees this as an opportunity to pick up support.”</p><p>The Data Center Coalition, the leading membership association for the data center industry, said the proposed one-year moratorium “sends another signal that Chicago is closed for business — both for data centers and for other significant economic development projects.</p><p>“It will cause Chicago to relinquish significant long-term economic investment, jobs and tax revenue to neighboring areas and states,” the coalition’s statement said.</p><p>Johnson countered that his only motivation is to “protect the health, safety and quality of life” for Chicago residents. “We welcome innovation, investment and the jobs and opportunities that come with it, but growth must be done responsibly,” the mayor said in a statement about the moratorium.</p><h3>Foundry Park TIF approved</h3><p>Council members also authorized a $201 million tax increment financing subsidy that would pave the way for JDL Development to start construction of the first phase of a $3 billion replacement for the failed Lincoln Yards mega-project on the North Side.</p><p>The <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/city-hall/2026/09/22/foundry-park-mega-project-tif-subsidy-finance-committee-approval" >Foundry Park subsidy</a> passed with support from Ald. Brian Hopkins (2nd), who dropped his opposition after city officials pledged that infrastructure improvements promised to area residents as part of the Lincoln Yards project would ultimately be delivered. Hopkins said the $3 billion development will be built over the course of ten years and, "We have time to fix this."</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Enhancement-item" data-crop=""> <figure class="Figure"><a class="AnchorLink" id="image-9f0000" name="image-9f0000"></a> <picture data-crop="medium"> <source type="image/webp" width="490" height="275" data-srcset="https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/381da02/2147483647/strip/true/crop/7145x4010+0+378/resize/490x275!/format/webp/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2Fbd%2F0e%2F75ba7de542ba8f8456a12973e6c5%2Fcouncil-260924-06.jpg 1x,https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/f6d385e/2147483647/strip/true/crop/7145x4010+0+378/resize/980x550!/format/webp/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2Fbd%2F0e%2F75ba7de542ba8f8456a12973e6c5%2Fcouncil-260924-06.jpg 2x" data-lazy-load="true" srcset="data:image/svg+xml;base64,PHN2ZyB4bWxucz0iaHR0cDovL3d3dy53My5vcmcvMjAwMC9zdmciIHZlcnNpb249IjEuMSIgaGVpZ2h0PSIyNzVweCIgd2lkdGg9IjQ5MHB4Ij48L3N2Zz4=" /> <source width="490" height="275" data-srcset="https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/6742ce3/2147483647/strip/true/crop/7145x4010+0+378/resize/490x275!/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2Fbd%2F0e%2F75ba7de542ba8f8456a12973e6c5%2Fcouncil-260924-06.jpg" data-lazy-load="true" srcset="data:image/svg+xml;base64,PHN2ZyB4bWxucz0iaHR0cDovL3d3dy53My5vcmcvMjAwMC9zdmciIHZlcnNpb249IjEuMSIgaGVpZ2h0PSIyNzVweCIgd2lkdGg9IjQ5MHB4Ij48L3N2Zz4=" /> <img class="Image" alt="Ald. Brian Hopkins (2nd) chats with a reporter before the start of a Chicago City Council meeting at City Hall Wednesday.</p></figcaption><span class="line"></span><div class="Figure-credit"><p>Ashlee Rezin/Sun-Times</p></div></div> </figure> </div> </div><p>The Council gave final zoning approval to a new 1.2 million square foot hospital on Northwestern Memorial Hospital’s Streeterville campus, a new warehouse campus on the Southwest Side site now occupied by Ford City Mall, a new Amazon “last-mile” warehouse in Gage Park and a new five-story building in Lincoln Park that will allow Francis W. Parker School to expand enrollment by 125 students.</p><p></p><p></p><p> </p><h3>Other Council action</h3><p>A nearly $14 million settlement was approved to compensate two defendants framed for murders by corrupt Chicago police Det. Reynaldo Guevara, along with a $6 million payout to the family of a man killed in another police chase gone wrong.</p><p>Ald. Ray Lopez (15th) voted against the Guevara settlements, citing a deposition that former Cook County State's Attorney Kim Foxx gave in a lawsuit filed by another one of Guevara's alleged torture victims. In it, Foxx said she believed that both of the defendants in line for Wednesday's settlements were guilty even though she granted them certificates of innocence.</p><p>Ald. Anthony Beale (9th), the City Council’s most senior member, proposed a reduced starting salary of $120,000 for newly elected alderpersons. Right now, 29 alderpersons get salaries of $155,688 a year, while those who opted out of cost-of-living raises are paid $142,776 a year.</p><p>And Bridgeport Ald. Nicole Lee proposed City Council hearings on Amtrak’s plan to build a maintenance facility in her ward, near Rate Field where the White Sox play. Lee has been determined to prevent the Sox from leaving Rate Field for the South Loop under <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/white-sox/2026/09/05/new-sox-park-future-owner-announces-proposal-for-riverside-stadium-at-the-railyards" >a plan proposed</a> by Sox minority owner Justin Ishbia. That plan also entails the construction of the Amtrak maintenance site in Bridgeport.</p><p></p><p></p>

entries.title: Review: ‘The Humanities’ looks away from the campus culture wars it purports to interrogate
entries.summary: <p>Sometimes in theater, timing is everything. I've seen that work in a playwright's favor, such as a play about a Queen (“<a class="Link" href="https://www.wbez.org/theater-stages/2024/11/09/coronation-play-laura-winters-women-presidency-packs-a-punch-after-trumps-win" target="_blank" ><u>Coronation</u></a>” by Refracted Theatre), premiering in the weeks after Trump's 2024 election.</p><p>In other cases, writing plays on slippery and ever-changing contemporary themes can put pressure on the writer to do more to respond to the moment.</p><p>That's what happened the last time Zayd Ayers Dohrn premiered a play. “<a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/theater/2025/10/14/goodman-theatre-revolution-review-tom-morello-zayd-ayers-dorhn-chicago-stages" target="_blank" ><u>Revolution(s)</u></a>” opened at Goodman Theatre in the height of Operation Midway Blitz, and, despite the title, it failed to say anything revolutionary. </p><p>Dohrn, who commendably likes to write about current events, has a new play called "The Humanities," premiering at Victory Gardens, that takes place in the aftermath of a problematic speaker being invited to the fictional Lincoln University.</p><p>The problematic speaker, Luka (Daniil Krimer), is underwritten. We know he is a former student of a professor named Martin (Steve Pickering) and has been influenced by the professor's lectures. Martin gives one such lecture during the play about ideology and how groups have influence over individuals.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Enhancement-item" data-crop=""> href="https://victorygardens.org/event/the-humanities-world-premiere/" target="_blank" >Victory Gardens Theater,</a> 2433 N. Lincoln Ave.<br><b>Info:</b> Tickets from $25</div> </div><p>So much of the story builds towards Luka’s on-campus speech, yet the production doesn’t fully flesh out who he is, explicitly state his ideology or clearly explain why he became a provocateur in the first place. All of this seems to be skirted in favor of dissecting the blowback of the invitation itself. Quite frankly, that’s not as interesting.</p><p>The majority of the action revolves around how the campus faculty and students react to the invited speaker. The University ends up doing damage control, as the speech lands days before its $2.5B capital campaign. The students meanwhile gear up for a mass protest that leads to violence and arrests.</p><p>The production arrives in Chicago just days after the one-year anniversary of the death of college campus provocateur Charlie Kirk, whose “Prove Me Wrong Debates” at universities around the country made him a celebrity and a victim. Kirk was fatally shot while speaking at an outdoor event at Utah Valley University. It also premieres weeks after Milo Yiannopoulos, a former Breitbart News editor also known for speaking on college campuses, was deported.</p><p>And yet again, in the looming shadow of real world events, Dohrn’s work misses the mark. The production meanders its way to the big speech where the former student-turned-provocateur Luka argues he’s “not a white supremacist,” but a “western supremacist” who believes in democracy. The actual speech is much too tepid to cause protests even in this fictional world and is a misrepresentation of students who feel they must protest campus speakers in the actual world, especially around such topics as genocide, immigration and human rights.</p><p>In the dialogue, we hear accusations that colleges indoctrinate students, that they contribute to culture wars, and that campuses are no longer public squares for the debate of differing ideals. It’s a fair stance to take. But crafting a play around the blowback a university faces for inviting a speaker is much easier, and far less risky, than parsing why students feel the speaker is problematic and examining the complexities of conflicting ideas on stage.</p><p>There are productions that thread this needle well. Theater Wit recently staged Itamar Moses’ “The Ally.” In that play, a problematic speaker at a fictional university makes a lengthy argument on behalf of the State of Israel — which takes guts to stage in an American theater in a progressive city in 2026. His argument gets countered by a Palestinian student, born and raised in Gaza in a production that does more to take risks and give space to uncomfortable and polarizing opinions.</p><div data-lazy-load="true" src="data:image/svg+xml;base64,PHN2ZyB4bWxucz0iaHR0cDovL3d3dy53My5vcmcvMjAwMC9zdmciIHZlcnNpb249IjEuMSIgaGVpZ2h0PSIyNzVweCIgd2lkdGg9IjQ5MHB4Ij48L3N2Zz4=" > </picture> <div class="Figure-content"><figcaption class="Figure-caption"><p>Steve Pickering, Naomi Evans and Ernest Bentley in a scene from “The Humanities.”</p></figcaption><span class="line"></span><div class="Figure-credit"><p>Photo by Michael Brosilow </p></div></div> </figure> </div> </div><p>There are, however, bright spots in the production. The acting was stellar, led by Chicago theater vet Steve Pickering. He’s the aging college professor who sparks the action of the play when he invites a former student to speak on campus. Pickering displays an outstanding ability to incorporate character ticks, and subtle nuances in delivering lines with flair or different pitches of voice — things that may go unnoticed individually, but as a whole, build a character that is believable and lived-in. Bringing him back from retirement was a great choice.</p><p>Ernest Bently is masterful as Jonas, a young hotshot Ivy Leaguer whom Martin has hired as an assistant professor in his department. Jonas is ambitious, astute, and keenly aware of how the university is positioning him because of his race — going so far as agreeing to moderate the talk with Luka in exchange for a faster track to tenure.</p><p>One of the most interesting threads in the play is the love triangle between Jonas, Martin and Martin’s wife, Margot (Naomi Evans), an art professor. In an early scene, Margot propositions Jonas to join the couple for a sexual encounter — rather, Margot and Jonas will participate, with Martin watching. With all the shifting dynamics of race, power, and age (Martin and Margot being much older than Jonas), this throuple is a compelling part of the narrative. Here, director Edward Torres shines. The scenes with these actors, throughout the production, were some of the most riveting in the show.</p><p>“The Humanities” has terrific acting, interesting subplots and provides plenty of chuckles. But unfortunately for Dohrn, it’s an issue of production mistiming (to be fair, he wrote this in 2019). Crafting a story around campus culture wars without mentioning any significant topics of debate, while so many in the audience are collectively experiencing these things in our real lives, makes what ends up on stage feel hollow.</p>

entries.title: Bill 'Captain Fun' Linden, former Sun-Times page designer, dies at 79
entries.summary: <p></p><p></p><p></p><p>Bill Linden was a dispenser of gratis grins.</p><p>When he turned to look at you, a clown nose or a pirate's eye patch might be on his face.</p><p>He had drawers full of silly glasses and hats and owned a white Elvis Presley jumpsuit and a red Sgt. Pepper uniform.</p><p>Mr. Linden worked for the Chicago Sun-Times from 1969 to 1996 doing graphic design and page layout.</p><p>"It was a creative world in the art department — people sketching and setting up photo shoots. It doesn't exist anymore, but I liked to visit back then because compared to the pressure of the newsroom it was like a playground, or the circus, and Bill was like the ring leader," said former Sun-Times reporter Dave Hoekstra. </p><p>"There were no boundaries in having fun with him."</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Enhancement-item" data-crop=""> <figure entries.title: Former White Sox pitching coach Don Cooper, who led a World Series-winning rotation, dies at age 70
entries.summary: <p>KANSAS CITY, Mo. — Former longtime <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/white-sox" >White Sox</a> pitching coach Don Cooper has died at the age of 70, per a family announcement on social media. The team has confirmed the news.</p><p>Debuting with the Twins in 1981, Cooper pitched in parts of four MLB seasons before beginning his coaching career with the White Sox’ Single-A affiliate in 1988.</p><p>Cooper rose through the ranks of the team’s player development system until he was promoted to the role of major league pitching coach in July of 2002, when he replaced Nardi Contreras. From there began one of the most productive coaching runs in White Sox history.</p><p>Forever associated with the dominant starting rotation of the 2005 Sox team that captured the franchise’s only World Series title of the past 100 years, Cooper remained the club’s pitching coach until he was fired alongside manager Rick Renteria after the shortened 2020 campaign.</p><p>Cooper’s tenure included Esteban Loaiza’s second-place finish in Cy Young voting in 2003, Chris Sale’s five-straight All-Star appearances in a White Sox uniform, and the peak years of Mark Buehrle’s career, which included both his 2007 no-hitter and his 2009 perfect game. When Buehrle, Jose Contreras, John Garland and Freddy Garcia closed out the 2005 American League Championship Series with four-straight complete games, it was first time an MLB team had accomplished that feat in a single postseason since 1928, and none have managed it since.</p><p>From 2003, Cooper’s first full season, to his last in 2020, White Sox pitchers were fourth in MLB in wins above replacement (WAR), per FanGraphs.</p><p>Especially as major league pitching instruction has come to involve advanced technology, private coaches and data analysis, Sox pitchers reiterated that Cooper’s greatest strength lay in a building block of coaching: he instilled confidence in his players. At the height of his powers, as a collection of pitchers rose from obscurity to success like Loaiza’s 21-win campaign, Matt Thornton rise to becoming an All-Star reliever, or Phillip Humber throwing a perfect game in 2012, an enduring adage became popular among White Sox fans when addressing every new pitching addition:</p><p>“Coop’ll fix ‘em.”</p>

entries.title: Bears QB Caleb Williams is back to being a punching bag, but he's never let a little backlash get him down
entries.summary: <p>The Summer of Caleb Williams is over, ending as abruptly as the weather changed this week when summer itself ended.</p><p>As the hype ballooned for months amid expectations that he’d be an MVP candidate, <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/bears" target="_blank" >Bears</a> coach <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/bears/2026/09/11/as-engineer-and-artist-blend-styles-bears-ben-johnson-gets-goosebumps-about-future-with-caleb-williams" >Ben Johnson</a> touting all he believed Williams was capable of and appearing on the coveted Madden 27 cover, it was only going to take a bad game or an injury to deflate it. Both happened Sunday as Williams sputtered through a 9-3 loss to the Vikings and left in the fourth quarter with a hamstring injury.</p><p>Williams’ approval rating remains sky high in Chicago, but the national conversation flipped sharply on him. He’s always been a player that people love to hate, and his emotional reaction to the injury reignited that with accusations of being overdramatic.</p><p>Even the Merriam-Webster dictionary took a whack at the video of him fighting through tears to pump his fist to the crowd at Soldier Field as he was carted to the locker room with a post on X that captioned it, “Just spelled ‘conscientious’ correctly on the first try.”</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center><div class="Enhancement-item"> <div class="ExternalContent-wrapper" > <div class="TweetUrl"> <blockquote class="twitter-tweet"><p lang="en" dir="ltr">Just spelled ‘conscientious’ correctly on the first try. <a href="https://t.co/Whl3RazMOR">pic.twitter.com/Whl3RazMOR</a></p>— Merriam-Webster (@MerriamWebster) <a href="https://x.com/MerriamWebster/status/2102454130472046757?ref_src=twsrc%5Etfw">September 22, 2026</a></blockquote> <script async src="https://platform.x.com/widgets.js" charset="utf-8"></script> </div> </div> </div></div><p>Williams is clocking all of it without saying a word. He re-posted five items about it on his X account. In an interview with the Sun-Times last season, he said he saves negative items like that for motivation and entertainment and speculated about why he’s been a popular punching bag dating back to USC.</p><p>“I guess I do things differently — dress, play, all these different things, [painting] my nails or whatever,” he said. “I do some things that don’t harm anybody else, but things that other people don’t like and have strong opinions about.</p><p>“It’s all good with me. It’s fun to laugh at because it’s not real, it’s not true, so it’s just ... something to joke about. My friends and I get a kick out of it.”</p><p>They mocked him when he cried while hugging his mom after a loss at USC. They made a meal out of him writhing on the bench against the Vikings as a rookie after he’d taken yet another sack and was simply trying to find a comfortable position given his back pain.</p><p>Setting aside the predictable nastiness of social media, Williams has been hearing it from people who actually have a platform.</p><p>Former NFL linebacker Will Compton, co-host of the popular Bussin’ with the Boys podcast, ripped him for leaving on a cart for merely a hamstring injury, drawing a rebuke from ex-Bear Kyle Long. Another former linebacker Emmanuel Acho agreed, saying on his podcast that Williams’ reaction to the injury was over the top unless it was season-ending.</p><p>Acho’s brother, Sam, who played for the Bears a decade ago, criticized Williams’ leadership credentials last year because his socks weren’t pulled all the way up during a preseason game.</p><p>On the other side, ESPN’s Stephen A. Smith said the Bears would be lost without Williams — “No Caleb Williams, no Chicago Bears relevancy,” he declared — so not everyone is a hater.</p><p>The anti-Williams crowd got more fuel Monday night when Giants quarterback Jaxson Dart suffered what turned out to be a season-ending knee injury, but was still trying to stay in the game.</p><p>The reality is that Williams had no way of knowing how injured he was Sunday. All he knew for sure was something was very wrong in a very essential part of the body for an athlete.</p><p>“Everyone has an opinion of why he reacted a certain way,” Raiders star Maxx Crosby said on his podcast. “I’ve had one hammy thing, and that [stuff] will freak you the [expletive] out when it first happens... He probably imagined something really bad just happened and you have all these emotions.”</p><p>When Johnson spoke vaguely about his recovery and wouldn’t rule him out even for the game Monday against the Eagles, it inadvertently contributed to an assumption that the injury wasn’t that bad. Johnson was only trying to nod to Williams’ resilience.</p><p>“He wants to be out there on the grass going full speed, so it is a little more challenging to hold a guy back like that,” Johnson said Wednesday. “If you could build a player, that's what you'd want him to be like.”</p><p>Really, the Bears still might not know precisely how bad it is or how much time he’ll miss. It’s still possible he’ll be out several games.</p><p>Either way, the cloud he floated into the season on has evaporated. He’s back to being a guy that so many people seem to enjoy watching fail, which he doesn’t like, but can survive.</p><p>Williams has withstood just about everything in his first three NFL seasons, and along the way poked holes in pre-draft narratives that he was selfish, soft, un-coachable and more concerned with fame than being a great player. Every bit of that has turned out to be wrong.</p><p>But, as usual, the only way for him to mute it is to get back on the field and get back to winning.</p>

entries.title: Review: ‘Detroit 67’ at eta Creative Arts Foundation
entries.summary: <p>When the lights come up on the set of Dominique Morisseau’s “Detroit '67,” now playing at eta Creative Arts Foundation, the first sound the audience hears is The Temptations' 1966 hit “Ain’t Too Proud to Beg.”</p><p>The song works on two levels: It inspired Morisseau’s Tony-nominated jukebox musical, “Ain’t Too Proud: The Life and Times of The Temptations,” which propelled the Detroit native into national recognition as a playwright. The song also foreshadows the events of this historical family drama, which unfolds in the basement of two Detroit siblings in the summer of 1967 — the turntable, which is playing the song on a 45, skips and the song fades away, signaling the need for change. Or perhaps, an upgrade.</p><p>This production is the first of a new partnership that has landed <a class="Link" href="https://www.wbez.org/theater-stages/2024/09/23/pulse-theatre-beneath-the-willow-tree-chicago" target="_blank" ><u>Pulse Theatre Company</u></a> as the first company in residence at eta, which was founded on the South Side in 1969. It launches a season that artistic director Aaron Reese Boseman says focuses on mental health in Black homes.</p><div class="RatingCard Enhancement" data-module data-rating="3.0" data-align-center> <div class="RatingCard-title"> ‘Detroit '67’ </div> <div class="RatingCard-content"> <span class="RatingCard-star"> <span class="RatingCard-star-full"> <svg class=""> <use xlink:href="#icon-star"></use> </svg> </span> <span class="RatingCard-star-half"> <svg class=""> <use xlink:href="#icon-star"></use> </svg> </span> </span> <span class="RatingCard-star"> <span class="RatingCard-star-full"> <svg class=""> <use xlink:href="#icon-star"></use> </svg> </span> <span class="RatingCard-star-half"> <svg class=""> <use xlink:href="#icon-star"></use> </svg> </span> </span> <span class="RatingCard-star"> <span class="RatingCard-star-full"> <svg class=""> <use xlink:href="#icon-star"></use> </svg> </span> <span class="RatingCard-star-half"> <svg class=""> <use xlink:href="#icon-star"></use> </svg> </span> </span> <span class="RatingCard-star"> <span class="RatingCard-star-full"> <svg class=""> <use xlink:href="#icon-star"></use> </svg> </span> <span class="RatingCard-star-half"> <svg class=""> <use xlink:href="#icon-star"></use> </svg> </span> </span> </div> </div><p></p><div class="RichTextSidebarModule Enhancement" data-module data-align-center><a class="AnchorLink" id="module-540000" name="module-540000"></a> <div class="RichTextModule-items RichTextBody"><b>When</b>: Through Nov. 1<br><b>Where</b>: eta Creative Arts Foundation, 7558 S. South Chicago Ave.<br><b>Tickets</b>: $25-$40<br><b>Info</b>: <a class="Link" href="https://www.pulsetheatrechicago.org/" target="_blank" >pulsetheatrechicago.org</a><br><b>Run time:</b> 2 hours, 30 minutes</div> </div><p>“Detroit '67,” the first play of Morisseau’s trilogy, The Detroit Project, follows siblings Chelle (Shenise Danyél) and Lank (Tamarus Harvel), who received an inheritance and a home from their late parents. The siblings use their basement to host unlicensed “after-hours” parties to earn extra cash. It takes place in the sweltering summer of 1967, when the city was deeply strained by racial segregation, housing discrimination and hostile police practices.</p><p>The production boasts a run time of over 2½ hours, which is long for my taste, but the story is layered and complex. Much of Act 1 examines the conflict between the siblings. Chelle, a widow supporting a son in college, is content hosting parties and keeping the nest egg from their parents as a rainy day fund. Meanwhile, the ambitious Lank, reminiscent of Walter Lee Younger in “A Raisin in the Sun,” insists they need more. His best friend Sly (Dairyon Bolden) has a tip on a bar for sale and encourages Lank to use the inheritance money to buy the business and go legit with the parties.</p><p>The questions that emerge here go much deeper than siblings having a difference of opinion. Lank is a dreamer and wants to see Black people have a real stake in Detroit, and views entrepreneurship as essential to that vision. Chelle believes the inheritance and home their parents left behind is itself a legacy.</p><p>More than being simply reluctant to buy the bar, Chelle seems opposed to change. Danyél is on an emotional roller coaster in this role and is a force in opposing Lank to follow his dreams, spurning Sly’s advances of love and even refuses to use the 8-track player Lank enthusiastically brings to the basement.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Enhancement-item" data-crop=""> <figure class="Figure"><a class="AnchorLink" id="image-110000" name="image-110000"></a> <picture data-crop="medium"> <source type="image/webp" width="490" height="275" class="Figure-content"><figcaption class="Figure-caption"><p>In “Detroit 67,” Chelle seems opposed to change while her brother, Lank, is a dreamer who insists they need to do more than the unlicensed “after-hours” parties they hold in their basement. </p></figcaption><span class="line"></span><div class="Figure-credit"><p>Aaron Reese Boseman</p></div></div> </figure> </div> </div><p>With all of this happening, a new character emerges: a bloody and battered white woman, carried in by Lank and Sly. She’s unconscious. And as mentioned above,<i> it’s 1967</i>. This is a big problem for the siblings.</p><p>The second act is a major pivot. The sibling rivalry takes a turn when Lank, obviously, spends the inheritance money on the bar behind Chelle’s back. But racial tensions between police and Black residents hinted at earlier in the play have now erupted into riots. The bar Lank and Sly just bought is now at risk of being burned down.</p><p>The white woman, Caroline (Emma Jean Eastlund), is on the run from the police. Her bruises, we learn, are the result of domestic violence from a cop she was dating. This also puts Chelle and Lank at risk for harboring her, further complicating the underlying racial tensions of the play.</p><p>A lot happens in this production. And the action, through both acts, is confined to the basement. Boseman directs, and has a clear comfort with Morisseau’s script (he recently directed Morisseau’s “Confederates” at Redtwist, a production that starred Danyél). The pacing allows for silence and space for characters to sit in emotion.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Enhancement-item" data-crop=""> <figure class="Figure"><a class="Figure-content"><figcaption class="Figure-caption"><p>Emma Jean Eastlund portrays Caroline in “Detroit 67” at eta Creative Arts Foundation. </p></figcaption><span class="line"></span><div class="Figure-credit"><p>Aaron Reese Boseman</p></div></div> </figure> </div> </div><p>Music at times feels like a character of its own. The sounds of Motown are a thread throughout with a soundtrack that features The Temptations, The Miracles and The Four Tops, among others. The music also helps manifest the themes of the production. In the opening scene, Chelle’s record player fails. Even with her record player broken, Chelle is not sold on the 8-track, insisting that hearing the scratch of a needle is an imperfection that enhances the experience of listening to music.</p><p>With riots outside and an unexpected visitor inside, Chelle is forced to come to grips with a changing world. The second act is filled with smoke, sirens and unrest, but through it all Chelle learns to dream, to love and to let go. She sheds her old record player, along with her old self, and in the final scene, pops The Four Tops into the 8-track player and dances freely. She’s a new woman.</p>

entries.title: Cubs, Red Sox to play Friday doubleheader as Boston weather forecast jumbles final-weekend series
entries.summary: <p>As the <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/cubs" >Cubs</a> face potentially the most meaningful games of their season, they’re facing some of the most uncertain scheduling of their season, too.</p><p>There’s <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/cubs/2026/09/22/cubs-noreaster-red-sox-boston-storms-rain-schedule-playoffs-shota-imanaga-jed-hoyer-justin-steele" >heavy rain projected this weekend in Boston</a>, where the Cubs will take on the Red Sox, and that forecast forced a doubleheader Friday – the games starting at 12:05 p.m. and 5:05 p.m. Central – with Sunday’s originally planned regular-season finale moved two days prior.</p><p>Saturday night’s game is currently slated to be played as scheduled, at 6:15 p.m. Central.</p><p>But the Cubs, who woke up Wednesday in a three-way tie in the NL wild-card standings and figure to be playing for home-field advantage in an opening-round playoff series this weekend, need to be ready for anything.</p><p>That might still include Major League Baseball finding a new venue for a game or multiple games, should they get washed away. While that doesn’t seem to be the first choice, hence the rescheduling announced Wednesday, the calendar is real; there’s only one day between the end of the regular season Sunday and the start of the postseason Tuesday.</p><p>“There’s still a lot of things on the table, for sure,” manager Craig Counsell said Wednesday. “What I know is happening is we’re going to play three games. If weather is an issue, we’re going to have to figure out a place to play a third game. We might have to figure out a place to play more than one game.”</p><p>While rainouts and reschedulings are a pretty normal part of a game played outdoors, it’s the timing that presents a potentially sizable hurdle for the Cubs to clear.</p><p>The circumstances mean this weekend’s games are far from just what’s left on the schedule. The Cubs’ eventual playoff seed remains a mystery and could still be one come Friday, Saturday, Sunday or beyond, depending on what happens with the weather. They could host an opening-round, best-of-three series at Wrigley Field or travel to play the Phillies, Padres or Braves on the road.</p><p>That’s a lot on the line.</p><p>“You’ve got to beat your opponents, and you’ve got to beat the circumstances sometimes, too, around everything,” Counsell said. “That’s part of this journey with your team. So it’s the next one in front of us.”</p><p>Particularly troublesome is how the team will deploy its pitching staff in meaningful games while still attempting to line up their preferred arms for the playoffs.</p><p>The Cubs will not have a rested member of their rotation at their disposal for one of the games in Boston. Right-hander Clay Holmes and lefty David Peterson are expected to go in the doubleheader, but the other three starters would be on short rest Saturday, leaving the Cubs scratching their heads over how to fill that other slot.</p><p>Might it be a bullpen day, difficult to engineer with so many arms needed for Friday’s twin bill? Might lefty Shota Imanaga, who would have been available to start on regular rest for the originally scheduled season finale Sunday, be forced to the mound? Might a roster move be necessary, with September rules preventing the addition of an extra player for doubleheaders?</p><p>“They never move games up, especially within a five-day window of a starting rotation,” Counsell said. “We can’t have somebody ready to pitch on Saturday. They just moved games up on us.</p><p>“I understand there’s extenuating circumstances, but you don’t see that happen.”</p><p>Here’s another wrinkle: The final game of the Cubs’ season, should the rains allow it to be played Saturday, will come a day before those of the Phillies and Padres. Typically, all of those final-Sunday games are played at the same time.</p><p>The Cubs could be going all out, using whatever pitchers they need to try to win Saturday. If the dust is settled on the wild-card race by Sunday, then, the Phillies and Padres could better align their pitchers for opening-round series, perhaps one coming against the Cubs.</p><p>It’s all part of the “what if” that’s hanging over the Cubs as they approach a weekend full of potentially high-impact games that could determine where and who they play in the postseason – details that could obviously affect how long they stay in the postseason.</p>
