entries.title: Why hasn't PGA Tour visited Chicago much lately until Presidents Cup?
entries.summary: <p>Since the Chicago area last hosted a PGA Tour event, NASCAR has been here more than the pro-golf circuit.</p><p>Think about that.</p><p>Nothing against stock-car racing, but it doesn’t have the connection here that golf does. Golf courses and driving ranges in the metropolitan area total in the hundreds. Good luck getting a last-minute tee time or bay on a beautiful day. It feels like everyone is playing golf around here.</p><p>Except the PGA.</p><p>Yes, it’s here this week at Medinah Country Club for the Presidents Cup — a team event pitting American players against internationals in a knock-off of the Ryder Cup — but it’s the first PGA event in the area since the 2023 BMW Championship at Olympia Fields.</p><p>We had the Western Open for much of its 100-plus-year history, which predated the PGA. In 2007, that became the BMW Championship and joined the FedEx Cup playoffs. It rotated among several courses, mostly in our area.</p><p>But in the last six years, that 2023 event has been the only one here.</p><p>“It seems like a no-brainer that we should be here more often than we are,” U.S. Presidents Cup captain Brandt Snedeker said Tuesday at Medinah. “That's something the new Tour staff is looking heavily at. I know Brian and his team have done a great job of trying to rethink how we do things and trying to have great places like this on the map for us.”</p><p>Brian is Brian Rolapp, the new PGA Tour CEO. He came from the NFL, where he spent 22 years, most recently as the league’s chief media and business officer. Before The Players Championship in March, Rolapp said he’s looking to host events in the country’s largest media markets that aren’t on the PGA’s schedule, and he included Chicago.</p><p>“Very golf-savvy town,” International captain Geoff Ogilvy said. “There's a big section of the Tour that would love to come back to Chicago every year. Chicago deserves a golf tournament. It's got great golf courses and great fans.”</p><p>Indeed, but these days, hosting a tournament is an enormous undertaking for those courses. A walk around Medinah Course No. 3 showed the results of construction practically everywhere. The first tee has stadium seating for 5,000, and suites are scattered across the course.</p><p>“We started building in April; we finished building three days ago,” said Joie Chitwood, Presidents Cup executive director. “That's six months of building out on this course. We’ll be open for six days, and it's three months to tear it down. So nine months of us working on the course and doing these things as members are enjoying their club.”</p><p>Granted, this is a Ryder Cup-level event. But even an event such as the BMW Championship can be enough of an inconvenience without enough of a benefit that club members pass on hosting. Conway Farms, which hosted the BMW in 2013, ’15 and ’17, didn’t get the bang for its buck, and membership has discussed whether it wants the event back.</p><p>That’s why the PGA Tour owns 30 properties across the country. TPC (Tournament Players Club) courses are run by the PGA, and though most are private, the circuit can do with them as they please. Illinois doesn’t have a TPC course.</p><p>“It is very challenging for a membership in a club to say, ‘We want to do this every year,’ because with winter, you're basically under construction every day the course is open,” Chitwood said. “There's a balancing act of how we can be in this market, but also at the right venues. I think that's the real key element.</p><p>“I would tell you, I’m so pleased with our results. And we are sharing those with our executive leadership, as we all identify that Chicago’s a fantastic market. It’s just hosting a PGA tournament is not easy for any community.”</p><p>Sponsorships play an integral role, too. BWM, for example, wants its event to be in an area that fits its brand. Title sponsorships for a standard annual event can cost roughly $15 million, and a top-tier event can be double that. Would a Chicago company want to help bring an event here?</p><p>We know this much: The players would love it.</p><p>“It would be really nice to get another tournament here,” said Scottie Scheffler, U.S. team member and the Tour money leader this year at more than $30 million. “With the size of the city and the amount of really good golf courses, that would be something that I think the Tour would be able to accomplish. I'm hoping for that in the future.”</p><p>“There’s so many great golf courses,” said teammate Corey Connors. “When Chicago is on the schedule, I’m looking forward to coming here and playing. Certainly this week is no different, but it’s a great sports city, and it’s a city I think that the PGA Tour should be at every year.”</p><p>The Tour is working it.</p><p>“It’s not like we don’t want to be here,” Chitwood said. “It’s just the fact that it’s a challenge and a market with a limited window to build and operate where you’re not so disruptive.”</p>

entries.title: Chicago School Board member Jessica Biggs faces scrutiny over 2018 firing as she runs for president's seat
entries.summary: <p><i>This story was reported and published in </i><a class="Link" href="https://www.chalkbeat.org/chicago/2026/09/23/jessica-biggs-firing-shadows-cps-school-board-president-race/" target="_blank" ><i>collaboration with Chalkbeat Chicago</i></a><i>.</i></p><p>Jessica Biggs holds up her work leading a South Side elementary school as a top reason voters should pick her in an intense fourway race for Chicago’s first elected school board president.</p><p>That’s even though she was fired from that job as principal at Burke Elementary in 2018, and until recently, was banned from working in Chicago Public Schools.</p><p>Biggs, a current school board member, has long maintained she was terminated based on a rushed internal investigation after openly criticizing problematic district practices — a claim she doubles down on in a <a class="Link" href="https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=_vrGpPMX1eA&t=7s" target="_blank" ><u>TV ad she released this week</u></a>.</p><p>But all three opponents in the race to lead the 21-member school board have highlighted her dismissal, arguing it’s disqualifying. Candidate Sendhil Revuluri said the investigation found “a deliberate, multi-year scheme to falsify attendance data to game her school's rating.” Opponents have also questioned whether Biggs’ removal from the Do Not Hire list last summer involved quid pro quo with district Superintendent Macquline King — a suggestion Biggs and King have strongly denied.</p><p>A close Chalkbeat and WBEZ review of the 2018 district inspector general’s report, CPS data, and all available court records, including transcripts, and interviews with at least a dozen district officials, educators, experts, and others show a more nuanced picture: At Biggs’ direction, Burke staff improperly marked students tardy when they arrived late enough that they should have been flagged as absent for half the day. An uptick in the school’s attendance rate under Biggs helped improve a high-stakes rating given to the school at the time. But the OIG report does not lay out a full-blown conspiracy to cheat, and it’s hard to say how much of the attendance bump came from mislabeling students versus a concerted effort to get kids to school. The watchdog recommended that Biggs be disciplined, but did not suggest she be fired.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Enhancement-item" data-crop=""> <figure how she did it after previous denials.</p></figcaption><span class="line"></span><div class="Figure-credit"><p>Victor Hilitski/For the Sun-Times</p></div></div> </figure> </div> </div><p>Former CPS CEO Janice Jackson stands by the decision to fire Biggs. But now, Jackson supports Biggs’ campaign to lead the school board, saying she has been impressed with her school board service.</p><p>“She didn't come back with a chip on her shoulder,” Jackson said. “She came back to serve and did the same thing she did when she was a principal, which was to look out for the kids and the families that she was entrusted with.”</p><p>The timeline of Biggs’ removal from the Do Not Hire list does not support the quid pro quo allegation, but there are unanswered questions about how she got off the list after a previous request was denied citing “serious” findings in the inspector general report. The reversal came eight months after Biggs started serving on the school board.</p><p>At a forum last week, Biggs said the allegations in the watchdog report “were around minor bureaucratic issues.”</p><p>“I have always said that this was unjust,” she said of her firing, adding that she was proud the Do Not Hire designation was removed.</p><h3>Concerns about attendance-tracking, student transportation led to Biggs’ firing </h3><p>Biggs took the helm at Burke Elementary in Washington Park in 2012 at a particularly contentious time. A former teacher, Biggs took on Burke as her first principalship after serving as an apprentice leader for a year at a different CPS school.</p><p>In her first year, Burke — serving about 270 mostly Black and low-income students — was on a list of 129 schools facing closure. It survived, but was then designated to take in students from a nearby shuttered school.</p><p>At the time, principals were under intense pressure to improve their schools, even as they had to make do with less amid recurring budget crises. Schools were given number ratings that carried high stakes, driving parents’ school choices and even district decisions about closures.</p><p>During the 2016-17 school year, a staffer complained to the district’s internal watchdog that Biggs was directing the attendance clerk to misrepresent attendance data and sent staff to pick up students in their personal vehicles without getting written permission from parents, as was CPS policy. One of her opponents, Hilario Dominguez, said this failure to follow transportation protocols “endangered students.”</p><p>The inspector general’s office substantiated the complaint after interviewing teachers, clerks, and other staff. Burke’s assistant principal told the watchdog that even a student who arrived 30 minutes before the end of the school day might still be marked tardy instead of absent. Illinois law requires that students attend for at least 300 minutes to be considered present.</p><p>Investigators suggested in their report that the school’s flawed tracking of attendance was tied to efforts to better its standing. In one email highlighted in the report, Biggs thanked school staff for their hard work to improve attendance and said that to boost the school’s rating, “we MUST hit 94% by the end of the year!” One teacher told the watchdog that staff felt pressure to increase attendance.</p><p>The inspector general’s office acknowledged it could not determine how widespread the tardy mislabeling was. But it noted Burke’s tardy count was four times the district’s average in 2016 and 2017. Staff at Burke logged more than 10,000 tardies in each of those two years and less than a dozen half-day absences.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Enhancement-item" class="Figure-content"><figcaption class="Figure-caption"><p>Jessica Biggs currently represents a school board district that stretches from the Loop down the lakefront to Woodlawn. She’s one of four candidates vying to become the first elected school board president.</p></figcaption><span class="line"></span><div class="Figure-credit"><p>Anthony Vazquez/Sun-Times file</p></div></div> </figure> </div> </div><p>Even before the watchdog’s investigation, Biggs’ supervisor had instructed the school not to mark students arriving really late as tardy.</p><p>In an interview with Chalkbeat and WBEZ, Biggs said she owns some of the report’s findings.</p><p>She admitted that she failed to keep proper documentation on student rides. Biggs said she likely reviewed driver’s licenses and insurance for staffers giving student rides, though she told the OIG in 2018 she was not aware she needed to verify them. But Biggs said her team was simply trying to help out families struggling with transportation, including some living farther away that enrolled at Burke after the school closures.</p><p>She acknowledged that some students were marked tardy who should have been designated as absent half a day. But she dismissed the idea that she oversaw an intentional plot to fudge attendance data. She said the district gave schools some leeway to determine when a tardy becomes a half-day absence. Biggs also noted schools with earlier start times, like Burke, tended to see many more late arrivals.</p><p>During Biggs’ six-year tenure, Burke’s attendance went from 88.1% in 2012 — a tough school year when a newly hired Biggs and her team battled closure — to 93.7% her last year in charge. The school's rating got a boost from state test score growth and a positive school climate survey, but the attendance rate remained consistently shy of the school’s 94% goal that would have pushed the rating up further. The year after Biggs was fired, the attendance rate dipped to 89.5% — a drop she attributes to staff turnover.</p><p>Stephanie Garrison, who taught at Burke for almost 20 years and is now retired, said she was concerned about student safety when she realized Biggs was telling employees to pick up children without following the required steps.</p><p>Garrison, a former union representative in the school, said some staff complained about Biggs’ “my way or the highway” attitude.</p><p>“The administration sets the tone,” said Garrison, who responded to outreach from WBEZ through the union. “There were a number of talented teachers that felt they had to really just move on.”</p><p>The teachers union backs Dominguez, Biggs’ opponent in the board president race.</p><p>Ever since her 2018 termination, Biggs has insisted she became a target because she complained about her school being dirty and that it was not being given enough special education staff or resources — two major controversies under then-Mayor Rahm Emanuel. During summer break after her firing, parents, staff, and community partners came out in support of Biggs at a meeting with school officials and questioned their motivation for letting her go.</p><p>Matt Lyons, who led the district’s talent office at the time of Biggs’ firing, said he didn't see evidence in the OIG’s investigation that she had intentionally manipulated attendance data.</p><p>Lyons said Biggs was not fired for speaking out but noted that her firing came in the months following an explosive <a class="Link" href="https://graphics.chicagotribune.com/chicago-public-schools-sexual-abuse/index.html" target="_blank" ><u>Chicago Tribune series about systemic failures to address sexual misconduct in</u></a> the district. While Biggs’ case had nothing to do with sexual misconduct or the Tribune’s reporting, Lyons maintains she faced harsher discipline because of the spotlight the report placed on CPS practices.</p><p>“It was a time of heightened scrutiny, and we felt public pressure to ensure school leaders were following policies by the book,” he said.</p><h3>Biggs’ removal from Do Not Hire list raises questions </h3><p>Biggs spent years working to clear her name after she was fired. She filed a lawsuit against CPS months after her 2018 firing, claiming that her firing violated her due process rights and stunted her education career. The court dismissed it because she had been an at-will employee and it found she failed to prove her firing prevented her from getting another job.</p><p>Later, in 2023, she asked CPS to remove the Do Not Hire designation in her employee file because it prevented her from volunteering to chaperone her daughter’s field trip. An internal CPS committee reviewed her request and allowed her to volunteer, but declined to make her eligible for employment.</p><p>In July 2024 after filing to run for school board, Biggs asked again. She cited her work on coordinating the city’s response to the COVID-19 pandemic and vaccination efforts with the nonprofit Southwest Organizing Project.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> data-lazy-load="true" src="data:image/svg+xml;base64,PHN2ZyB4bWxucz0iaHR0cDovL3d3dy53My5vcmcvMjAwMC9zdmciIHZlcnNpb249IjEuMSIgaGVpZ2h0PSIyNzVweCIgd2lkdGg9IjQ5MHB4Ij48L3N2Zz4=" > </picture> <div class="Figure-content"><figcaption class="Figure-caption"><p>Jessica Biggs spoke with voters outside Mollison Elementary on Election Day in 2024, when she first won election to the school board.</p></figcaption><span class="line"></span><div class="Figure-credit"><p>Ashlee Rezin/Sun-Times file</p></div></div> </figure> </div> </div><p>The district, under then-CEO Pedro Martinez, referred the petition to an outside law firm, likely to avoid conflict of interest concerns. In a detailed, five-paragraph letter, attorney Elizabeth Babbitt denied the request, saying the misconduct outlined in the OIG report was “serious.”</p><p>“At your direction, a CPS school manipulated attendance data and placed students' safety at risk by failing to comply with the CPS student travel policy,” Babbitt wrote.</p><p>In July 2025, Biggs tried a final time, arguing that her situation had changed because, in 2024, 40,000 voters elected her to the school board.</p><p>“I felt like it was an opportunity to right a wrong that had existed for a long time,” she said in the Chalkbeat/WBEZ interview.</p><p>The district, led by then-interim CEO Macquline King, turned to Babbitt again. A month later, the lawyer wrote a three-sentence letter to Biggs approving her removal from the Do Not Hire list. It did not contain a reason.</p><p>Babbitt did not respond to questions from Chalkbeat and WBEZ.</p><p>Lyons, the former HR chief at CPS, backed Biggs’ final successful attempt to get off the Do Not Hire list. In a letter, he wrote the OIG report detailed only “minor policy violations” that didn’t harm students and said Biggs was “widely regarded as a strong and beloved school leader.” More recently, he has donated to her bid for school board president.</p><p>Andre Smith, who lost to Biggs in the 2024 school board election and has been working for Victor Henderson, another candidate for school board president, said he is suspicious of the timing and the outside lawyer’s about-face. Smith is calling on the Cook County State’s Attorney, the CPS inspector general, and others to investigate.</p><p>He said it would be easy for a government investigation to pull phone and text messages to ensure there was no collusion between Biggs and King or other district leaders.</p><p>In a statement, CPS officials said “King did not review or decide any of the Do Not Hire petitions involving Ms. Biggs.”</p><p>That fall, the superintendent search committee led by Biggs voted not to include King on a list of finalists. Biggs said that’s evidence there was no quid pro quo.</p><p>The search then stalled, and Biggs distanced herself from it. In March of this year, Biggs eventually voted with 17 other school board members to give King the permanent position.</p><p>Sean Harden, the current appointed school board president, said he doesn’t think “anything malicious or untoward” happened. But “it probably would have been best practice” for Biggs to notify the school board that her Do Not Hire designation had been lifted before she voted to hire King.</p><p>Biggs said she didn’t bring it up because there was no conflict in her vote for King since a third party decided to remove her from the list.</p><p>Jonathan Collins, a school board expert at Columbia University’s Teachers College who also serves on New York City’s appointed school board, said Biggs’ case put CPS in a tough spot.</p><p>Outsourcing doesn’t completely ward off the perception that a board member leveraged her position, he said. But having a board member barred from working for the district makes for “terrible optics.”</p><p>“It’s a lose-lose situation,” he said.</p><p>As the next school board president is about to take over, principals are once again under pressure to increase attendance. CPS has struggled to recover from a pandemic-era absenteeism jump.</p><p>Asked how she would approach the case of a school leader accused of manipulating data, Biggs said she would take the allegations seriously. But she’d also interrogate the charges and focus on due process for principals.</p><p>“I think one of the most important levers for change in the district is really strong principal leadership, and we ask our principals to do a lot, and they need to be protected in their jobs,” Biggs said. “I'm also aware that humans, government entities, are fallible, and so it's why it's important to read documentation that comes before us to ask questions to push back.”</p><p><i>Mila Koumpilova is Chalkbeat Chicago’s senior reporter covering Chicago Public Schools. Contact Mila at mkoumpilova@chalkbeat.org. </i></p><p><i>Sarah Karp is an education reporter for WBEZ, part of Chicago Public Media. Contact Sarah at skarp@wbez.org.</i></p>

entries.title: How the Blackhawks used analytics to shape their goalies' offseason training
entries.summary: <p>Shortly after last season ended, <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/blackhawks" target="_blank" >Blackhawks</a> goalie Arvid Soderblom received a data dump.</p><p>Although Soderblom was coming off a subpar season, the data was not intended to critique him.</p><p>Instead, it was intended to supplement his offseason training. It contained information about where the shots he faced came from and how he fared against shots from each location.</p><p>"That was cool to see," Soderblom said. "I've never gotten that before. That was something I could use [with] the goalie coach, when we were setting up drills, to go from the data and build shooting drills from that."</p><p>Hawks starting goalie Spencer Knight, coming off a <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/blackhawks/2026/09/19/blackhawks-spencer-knight-nhl-goalies-luukkonen-shesterkin" >stellar season</a>, received a similar data dump. So did AHL goalie Drew Commesso.</p><p>One of the main takeaways: All three goalies should focus on lateral movement and, in general, saving shots that followed east-west passes.</p><p>"You can see what we give up as a team, how we defend, how we play certain things," Commesso said. "If you're able to zone in on what you give up primarily, it gives you a summer like I had."</p><p>The Hawks have employed one of the NHL's larger analytics departments for several years now, but they've been somewhat secretive about what that department builds and how the overall organization uses those tools.</p><p>In hockey media, analytics are often used for player and team evaluation, assessing who's good and who isn't. Presumably, the Hawks' front office does use them in the same way when making contract and trade decisions.</p><p>But analytics can be useful on a more micro level, too, to help existing Hawks players get better.</p><p>Coach Jeff Blashill has demonstrated interest in the science of analytics and the potential advantages it creates, but he's discerning nonetheless about which analytics measure what they're supposed to — and which don't. </p><p>His recent comments about the currently available analytics not assessing players' defensive acumen as accurately as their offensive acumen stirred up debate in the community.</p><p>In this case, after the Hawks' analytics department gathered the goaltending data, Hawks goalie coach Jimmy Waite and goalie scout Dan Ellis compared the numbers to raw video to verify their accuracy and relevance. Only once satisfied did they distribute the data to Knight, Soderblom and Commesso.</p><p>"I'm not an expert in data science, [but] I've been around enough people to know there are certain [analytics] that are much more predictive," Blashill said.</p><p>"Scoring off the pass [and] scoring off east-west plays is very predictive. Your shooting percentage goes way up, no matter who you are as a player. That [analytic] is good."</p><p>That's not a new revelation. Former NHL goalie Steve Valiquette published an <a class="Link" href="https://cdn1.sportngin.com/attachments/document/0137/7547/The_Royal_Road_-_Scoring.pdf" target="_blank" >article</a> about it in 2014 after tracking goals preceded by passes that crossed from one side of the net to the other, forcing the goalie to move side-to-side. He called it the "royal road," and that term stuck.</p><p>Blashill noted the recent league-wide movement toward diamond-shaped penalty kills, for example, stems from a desire to take away those "royal road" passes.</p><p>It is especially important for Hawks' goalies to keep that fact in mind, however, because the young defense in front of them allowed opponents to complete east-west passes relatively often last season.</p><p>"That’s not necessarily because of the system," Blashill said. "We just didn’t do a good enough job [defending] those. That’s an area we want to eliminate more of those."</p><p>Commesso regularly sent videos of himself to Ellis and received feedback to share with his own coach at home in Massachusetts. He worked on stopping movements and changing directions faster.</p><p>And in Sweden, Soderblom worked on being patient and springy on his feet, which should help him explode across the crease more swiftly and powerfully when necessary.</p><p>"Like a boxer or soccer goalie, they're light on their feet and really quick," Soderblom said. "You can't dig in too much on the ice."</p>

entries.title: In Gary, Indiana, a month after historic NIPSCO power outage, families still wait for relief
entries.summary: <p>Inside Melissa Dixon’s home in Gary, the lights are back on. Her refrigerator is working. And she’s playing music as she does yard work. The generator that she had on her front steps is gone now. </p><p>It's more than a month since Dixon and hundreds of thousands of others in Gary and across northwest Indiana were left without power, some for at least <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/graphics/weather/powerless/12-nights-without-power-in-Gary-Indiana/" target="_blank" ><u>two weeks</u></a>, and she's still feeling anxious.</p><p>It wasn’t until recently that she finally did a big grocery haul. Until then, she'd been buying only enough food for a day or two.</p><p>“I don’t want to put food in here or buy food for a couple days,” Dixon says, “because I don’t want to lose my food again.”</p><p>She was among nearly 375,000 of the Northern Indiana Public Service Company's customers — of the 500,000 it serves — who were without electricity for days after an Aug. 11 derecho. </p><p>Gusts of 99 miles an hour were recorded at the Gary/Chicago International Airport. But Gary was one of the last communities to have power fully restored, U.S. Rep. Frank Mrvan, D-Indiana, whose congressional district includes Gary, said in a letter to the Federal Energy Regulatory Commission asking for a federal <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/2026/08/31/indianas-governor-demands-probe-of-power-utility-during-tour-of-storm-ravaged-gary" target="_blank" ><u>investigation</u></a> of NIPSCO’s response.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Enhancement-item" data-crop=""> <figure class="Figure"><a class="AnchorLink" id="image-0e0000" name="image-0e0000"></a> <picture The church organized food giveaways and opened to neighbors who were without power. Now, the Rev. Eric Boone, Tree of Life's senior pastor, says families in Gary are staying afloat, but things aren’t completely back to normal. Some people regained power only to find out their refrigerators no longer worked, he says.</p><p>“Even though lights came on, people’s bank accounts didn’t bounce back,” Boone says. “People’s food, refrigerators and freezers didn’t bounce back. Some people got mold. Some people’s houses are wrecked. Some people lost their cars.”</p><h3>Health worries</h3><p>Outside Dixon’s home, a large tree branch that had fallen on a neighbor’s property has been cut into smaller pieces. That's for firewood she plans to keep in case another storm knocks out the power again.</p><p>Inside, Dixon has stocked her refrigerator with staples like milk and eggs. She gets waffles to satisfy her four daughters, who range in age from 12 to 22 years old. Her younger daughters are all back in school. The house is mostly quiet with them in class. But steps from the kitchen, Dixon says she's worried about dark spots along the walls in her basement. Maybe those are mold. She keeps two dehumidifiers running in the basement, where she typically sleeps.</p><p>“We’re sick because of the mold,” Dixon says. “I started feeling really weird, like my vision … a lot of pain in my face and my neck area and going down my arm and my shoulder.”</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Enhancement-item" data-crop=""> <figure class="Figure"><a class="AnchorLink" Sun-Times</p></div></div> </figure> </div> </div><p>Dixon says she started to feel sick soon after the power was restored. She was taking medicine to try to treat inflammation that has led to facial nerve problems.</p><p>She'd like to move her family out of her home temporarily — until she’s able to get it checked for mold and any necessary remediation. </p><p>But first she needs some support. She applied for disaster relief through the Federal Emergency Management Agency, but her application is still pending.</p><p>The only financial help she has gotten is a $150 voucher from her township. Calling hotline after hotline has been like trying to win a contest rather than just get relief after a natural disaster.</p><p>“It’s like calling a radio station,” she says. “‘Ooh, am I going to win these tickets?’”</p><h3></h3><p>Dixon is among more than 33,000 people in Lake County, Indiana, who have applied for relief money from FEMA. The federal agency says $48.19 million has been allocated for Lake County but didn't say how many applications have been approved.</p><p>Gary officials distributed an additional $500,000 in disaster relief to about 1,200 households. In a city of about 67,000 people, that’s also only a fraction of the possible need.</p><p>Shanequa Cauley is among those in Gary who have struck out on getting help. She lost power for about nine days. It took much longer for her employer's power to be restored. That meant she lost out on about three weeks of pay.</p><p>Cauley says she borrowed from a friend to pay her rent on time. Some of the meals she and her 7-year-old daughter ate during the first weeks after the storm came from the City Life Center, which provided free hot meals to families in Gary. The center later gave out vouchers for $300 to use at a grocery store.</p><p>But those meals have since ended. Cauley is hopeful she can get her finances in better shape before the end of the month.</p><p>“I’m praying by next week everything should be good,” says Cauley, who <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/news/2026/08/25/nipsco-filed-application-for-customer-rate-increases-amid-storm-that-ravaged-northwest-indiana" target="_blank" ><u>owes NIPSCO</u></a> about $89. “The first thing I’m going to do is get my NIPSCO caught up.”</p><h3>‘Refuse to be knocked out’</h3><p>Britney Rice, community adaptation program manager for the American Red Cross in Indiana, says caseworkers have been trying to connect Gary residents with the resources they need. Twenty-eight people are still living in temporary shelter, according to Rice, who says the Red Cross also assisted others in getting vouchers from a state program to stay at a hotel for 30 days.</p><p>Some people haven’t been able to replace the food they lost during the outage. For others, the Red Cross is helping get them into a better situation than they were before the storms, which could include connecting them to other resources such as housing, Rice says.</p><p>“When people have been impacted by disasters and the trauma that goes along with it, and they kind of kick into survival mode, sometimes all they can see is what’s in front of them,” Rice says. “And they make decisions that, if they could have seen something much bigger, then they would have made bigger decisions.”</p><p>Boone says his Tree of Life congregation has been scrambling to get relief information out. There still are people trying to figure out how to get by, he says. But Boone says he’s been heartened by how people in Gary have come together.</p><p>“We are strong," Boone says. "We are some that don’t give in or give up easily.
